Prototype Home · Deals · deal detail · create/edit deal · lenders on a deal. Built from the LenderPrism repo at 9f3427fc — its tokens, its component metrics, its enums. Sign up / log in Broker profile
What is clickable, where every value comes from, and what we invented
  • Tokens are the repo's, copied not matched. apps/lender-prism/frontend/src/app/globals.css — --primary navy-900 rgb(1,39,88), --sidebar navy-950 rgb(8,20,45), --radius 0.5rem, the eight-step shadow ramp, --tracking-normal -0.011em.
  • Component sizes are the repo's too. Button h-9 / h-8 / h-6, rounded-md; Badge rounded-full px-2 py-0.5 text-xs; Card rounded-xl border shadow-sm; Table th h-10 px-2 font-medium; Input h-9; Checkbox size-4 rounded-[4px]; sidebar 3rem collapsed, menu buttons h-8 rounded-md p-2. One departure: the rail is drawn at 14rem, not the shipped 16rem — the widest thing in it is the org line, which truncates at either width, so the extra 32px was empty. Re-checked on 31 Aug when Leads became Opportunities (see the naming note below): at thirteen characters it is now the longest label by some way, and it still sets without wrapping or truncating, so the departure stands. Changing SIDEBAR_WIDTH in ui/sidebar.tsx is a one-line edit. [💡 rec] Chips were audited against the repo on 3 Sep and the geometry corrected: .pill and .more were --radius-sm squares against a Badge that is rounded-full, so both are pills now. Padding stays at 7px rather than Badge’s px-2 — the Figma table columns were measured against these widths and 2px a chip moves them. There is no Chip or Tag component anywhere in the repo — zero filename hits for either word across the monorepo; ui/badge.tsx is the whole vocabulary, and when the team needs a new one they add a variant to it (section, section-navy, section-gold are theirs, with #023E8A and #b48b2b hardcoded). Figma agrees: the Prism — Design System library returns no chip at all, and the only one attached to the Broker file is a / chips in Cieden’s generic wireframe kit. So every chip on this prototype is custom, and two of them say things the product does not. The overflow chip is the first. Ours is a dashed +2 more; the product’s is MultiSelectValue’s overflowBehavior, which measures the trigger and prints a solid Badge reading +2. Dashed is the better of the two — it reads as an affordance rather than a value, which is what it is — so the proposal is variant="more" on badge.tsx rather than CSS here or a silent divergence there. [💡 rec] The profile’s two chip fields are the second, and the bigger one. forms/signup/AreasOfFocusSection.tsx renders both states and property types through RHFMultiSelect → shadcn MultiSelect — a popover with a Command list and Badge chips in the trigger. This page draws neither that way: property types are an inline toggle grid, states are chips plus an + Add a state select. For property types that is deliberate [💡 rec] — 24 values in 5 named groups, and a popover hides the whole taxonomy behind a click, so the grid shows what a broker is choosing among; ui/toggle-group.tsx with type="multiple" is the component it should be built on, which is what the aria-pressed buttons here already are by hand. For states it is not defensible [~] — 50 values need search, the shipped control has it, and ours does not; matching production is the right call and has not been made yet.
  • The widest chip got its room back, 6 Sep (Tanya) — “Bridge / Short-Term Debt (<3 Yrs)” is the longest execution label and the pill caps at 210px, but the network table and the account roster gave the Execution type cell only 200px — less than the pill after cell padding — so the chip painted over the State column beside it. Both cells now carry the 230px the matches table already used for the same column: one label, one ceiling, measured against it everywhere it prints.
  • The responsive layer is ours; only the breakpoint is the repo's. There was nothing to copy — app/(dashboard)/my-deals/page.tsx carries two responsive utilities in 385 lines (sm:px-6, lg:px-8) over a plain desktop table, so below about 1100px the columns squeeze until deal names wrap one word per line. What the repo does settle is where mobile starts: hooks/use-mobile.ts MOBILE_BREAKPOINT = 768, and ui/sidebar.tsx swaps the rail for a Sheet at SIDEBAR_WIDTH_MOBILE = 18rem below it. Both are honoured — 767 is the phone edge and the rail becomes an 18rem overlay with a scrim. Above it, two steps of our own: at 1180 the fixed 1180 slab is released and tables scroll inside their card rather than squeeze; at 900 the page header, toolbar and two-column deal summary stack. Below 767 each table row becomes a labelled block — the column headings survive as the labels — and a board lane fills the screen. [💡 rec] [repo Aug 26]
  • Empty states became two shapes, 14 Sep [💡 rec] — Tanya, seeing the same absence drawn three different ways in one sitting: “we need to standardize the empty state UI and layout — keep 2 options, horizontal for sidebars and modals and vertical for pages?” Two is right. The surface is the wrong switch, and the file already routed against it in both directions: the horizontal band drew on full pages twice, for notes and deal history, while the vertical box drew inside a drawer. What actually predicts the usage is what the copy has to do. A teaching state explains why the region is empty and what would fill it, so it needs a measure, a centre and room for two sentences — .empty. An offering state names the absence and hands over the one control that ends it, so it earns a single band — .empty--inline. Surface correlates, because pages usually teach and sections usually offer, but it is a consequence rather than the cause, and routing on it picks wrong at both ends. [~] The audit found four shapes across twenty call sites, not two: the centred .empty at thirteen, a dashed .empty--box at one, the horizontal .lnempty at seven, and .empty2 — one bare grey sentence in the match preview — at one. Three of the thirteen hand-tuned their own padding (26, 34 and 38px), each right once, on one screen, and then no longer a decision anybody could see. Those collapse into a single size step, .empty--sm, which is what a card body or a drawer section gets and a page or tab body does not. The defect that started it was a misclassification, not a copy-length bug. Deal history taught — Deals appear here as you save this institution’s bankers to them — inside a shell built to offer, and at 862px its button wrapped onto a second row and stranded against the right edge with nothing above it, while No notes yet in the same class at the same width stayed one row at 54px. Reclassifying it removes the wrap by construction rather than by a character budget, and it costs 80px → 171px: a teaching empty state honestly takes that room. The edge is opt-in and it means something. Dashed is already this file’s border for a slot waiting to be filled — the dropzone, the photo tile, the blank source box — so .empty--slot goes on states a broker ends by putting something there. .empty--edge is solid, for a band stating a fact with nowhere to put anything. That distinction caught two impostors: the reveal-quota gates were never empty states at all. They wore .lnempty because it was the only horizontal shell in the file, and inherited a dashed border inviting a click that fills nothing — you cannot end a quota by putting something in it. They take the solid edge; the match-preview sentence takes no edge, because the panel around it already draws one. One row is now a contract the CSS can keep. The band aligns its actions with justify-content: space-between rather than margin-left: auto, which resolves per flex line: beside text the growing paragraph leaves no free space to distribute and the items stay packed with the buttons last, but alone on a wrapped line they sit at main-start — a stacked layout rather than a broken one. Measured at 1505px on all twenty sites. .lptail, the Contacts-card tail, carries the same strand risk and is left alone on purpose: it is a card tail, not an empty state. [~]
  • The sidebar is not a proposal — it already ships. components/app-nav-sidebar.tsx renders a collapsible rail for brokers today. What we changed is which items are in it: Lender Funnel is retired [agreed 14 Aug] and Deals takes its place. ⚠ The shipped rail already has an item called My Deals and it is a different object — the assigned-leads pipeline off /api/assigned_leads. That collision needs settling with the deal-object naming. The foot became two bands, 3 Sep [💡 rec] — the rail ends in a hairline, and until today that hairline fenced all three foot controls together: the Account destination, the credit balance and the identity trigger. Three different kinds of thing in one group, stating no relationship between them beyond not a deal, in the tallest single band in the rail at 142px. The line now sits one item lower, so it fences exactly one thing — below it is you, above it is everything you use — and the block under it is 73px. Account keeps its balance beside it, because the balance is a section of the page the link points to. Five partitions were drawn before this one was chosen [💡 rec · divider study]: Account alone above, Credits alone above, two hairlines with one item each, and the inversion that fences the credit box alone at the floor on the argument that it is the only control in the rail which spends money. That last is the one arrangement where the border on the box stops being an anomaly and becomes the point, and it is parked rather than dismissed: it puts an upsell directly below the broker’s own name and takes Sign out off the floor of the column, which nothing in the 3 Sep sweep of 36 products does, and whether credits are a growth surface is a commercial call nothing in the KB settles [~]. Two declarations moved, not a rewrite. margin-top: auto goes up with the promoted band, since it is the thing that eats the rail’s slack — left on the footer it would have floated Account and the balance up under Education and opened a gap above the identity block. And the credit box’s margin-bottom: 8px came off: it existed only to hold the box clear of the identity block, a job now done by the band’s own padding, the hairline and the footer’s padding. The promoted band takes the nav group’s 8px inset rather than the footer’s 12px, which carries a payoff worth the change on its own — Account’s icon and label now land on exactly the x of every nav row above them, 35px and 63px, matching Education to the pixel, where the footer inset had them 4px out. [~] The objection that survives the change: the credit box is still the only bordered element in the rail, and promoting it into the nav column makes that read louder rather than quieter. The fix is to stop drawing it as a box at all — the rail already owns a right-hand slot for a value, the one carrying Education’s ↗ — but that folds two controls into one, which is a different decision from where the line goes and is not taken here. Community joined Tools, 14 Sep [T · Figma comment, 9 Sep] — “Add a link to our community”, pinned on the Education row, with the URL. It is the second outbound item in the rail and it takes the same ↗: icon at x=35, label at 63, arrow at 217, identical to Education. The group was a labelled group of one until today, which stated a relationship to nothing; a second member is what makes the Tools label earn its 32px [~]. Labelled Community and not The Multifamily Zone, because the rail names what a thing is for and never a brand — a product name in that list reads as a fifth destination [💡 rec · label]. The glyph is two people rather than a speech bubble, because a bubble belongs to Messages — named in Tony’s Flow 01 and asked for again in this same comment set — and Community would have spent its glyph. Unlike Education it carries a real href with target=_blank: /education is the marketing shell and there is nothing to point at, this URL exists, and a new tab leaves the prototype standing mid-demo. Nothing below it moved — margin-top: auto on the promoted band eats the rail’s slack, so the extra row shortens the gap above Account instead of pushing the identity block off the floor. ⚠ Three of Tony’s calls would change this row and none is made: whether brokers land on the collection he gave or the network root, whether the space is one of the paid tiers the marketing footer prices — which would need a Pro pill rather than a plain link — and whether a signed-in broker carries their session into Mighty Networks or meets a second login.
  • Leads became Opportunities, 31 Aug [T] — Tony, sheet comment on the Naming & lexicon row, 28 Aug 01:02, answering “Lead and Opportunity are one object — pick one word”: “Let’s go with ‘Opportunity’.” The rail item is renamed and nothing else is. [~] Scope is the narrow reading of that answer: only the Lead object is renamed, so Deal, Loan Request, Transaction and Loan all stand, and the shipped My Deals item is untouched — the sheet row lists Deal and Lead as separate nouns, which is what makes the narrow reading available. The wide reading (Opportunity replaces the deal object on every screen) is a different and much larger change and has not been taken. The route stays /leads: a shipped path is not a user-facing noun, and changing it is a redirect rather than a naming decision. The collision this resolves [⚠ was] — Leads carried three meanings at once: this rail section (house-sourced borrower leads routed to the broker, the Pro tier’s headline [T · 26 Aug call]), the first lane of the deal board, and the retired object name. Two are now gone. What is left is the board’s first lane, which Tony named Leads in the same comment set: no longer a clash, but a word that would name a stage and nothing else in the product. [💡 rec] Rename it New — stage 2 is Screening, so New states what the stage is without borrowing the next lane’s word, and it retires Lead cleanly instead of leaving one behind. Done, same day (Tanya): DEAL_STATUS now opens with New, seeds and all, so the word Lead appears nowhere in the product. [💡 rec] and not a transcription — the other seven stages are Tony’s and stand as he set them, and this one is ours to propose, so it is his to reject. Deliberately not Opportunities: that is now the object’s name, and a deal sitting at stage Opportunities would put an object noun in a lane slot — the same category error as the collision this is fixing, pointed the other way. [~] One consequence worth raising with him: in Salesforce and HubSpot a Lead becomes an Opportunity as it qualifies, so naming the inbound object Opportunity while the working object stays Deal makes the pipeline read Opportunity → Deal, the reverse of the convention every broker arrives with. It is the client’s vocabulary to set; it is not a blocker; it should not be discovered after it is on every screen. He rejected the rec, 31 Aug call [T] — Tanya raised the lane naming on the call and Tony chose Leads: “just change the word new to leads”, with Opportunities staying in the navigation. His frame makes them different entities — an Opportunity is a potential lead awaiting acceptance; once the broker accepts it, the deal enters at Leads. Applied 2 Sep (Tanya): DEAL_STATUS, seeds and the create path now open with Leads. The Salesforce-convention consequence above still stands, sharpened — the word Lead is back in the product as a stage inside an object pipeline that starts at Opportunity.
  • Active nav tint is --sidebar-accent (navy-700), which is what SidebarMenuButton actually binds — not --sidebar-border. Collapse the rail with the control beside the wordmark.
  • One account menu, not two profile entries. The shipped app splits “you” across two surfaces: a Broker Profile nav item (/broker-profile, pro brokers only — the public directory listing: headshot, cover photo, submit for admin approval) and the top-bar dropdown (components/global/top-nav.tsx: Profile Settings → /profile, Sign out). Same word, two objects, two places. [💡 rec] consolidated here: the account button at the foot of the rail opens one menu — your name and sign-in address, then Your profile · Sign out — and the nav item is gone. The identity header follows the 3 Sep deep sweep: every avatar menu sampled (Hootsuite, Gemini, Copilot, Skillshare) opens with who you are, and the email is the one place the shell says which account Sign out will end. The routes stay separate; only the entry point merges.
  • The filters are the repo's own MultiSelect — ui/multi-select.tsx, a Popover over a Command list, selected values rendered as Badge variant="outline" inside the trigger with a +N overflow badge and a CheckIcon per row. One deviation: the field's name stays on the trigger, because the repo puts it in a Label above the field and a filter toolbar has nowhere to put one. Each option is counted live against the other filter — the number is not printed, but an option whose count is zero dims, so the dim means that combination is genuinely empty rather than that the value is unknown.
  • Property type is the canonical twenty-four, not the eight on this page [repo Aug 14] [T · Figma comment, 21 Aug] — the filter is pinned to PROPERTY_TYPES in packages/constants/index.ts, so it offers every type the product stores. A row dims only when your other filters empty it — a type no sample deal uses stays regular, because over a canonical vocabulary absence is the normal state, not a signal. Tony’s comment asks the filter to “match the property types we have for universal searches and lender criteria in all submission forms”; two things still disagree with it and neither is ours to settle. His own Zoho submission form carries 22 of these — no Build to Sell Single-Family & Condos, no Note Purchase Financing — and the shipped filter rail on My Deals and Lenders offers four coarse buckets (Multifamily · Commercial · Industrial · Retail) over rows that display the granular values. ⚠ Which list is the master is question 75. The eight group headings here are the rollup that lets one list serve both shapes — browse coarse, store granular — and they are [💡 rec] ours: they are not the seven licensable asset classes, which cover only eighteen of the twenty-four. The picker itself follows Janover Pro’s own property-type control [comp 28 Aug]: an accordion — group rows hold their place and expand beneath themselves with a child count and rotating chevron, several open at once, checkboxes on the granular values. Two departures from Janover, both Tanya’s (28 Aug): the group row carries its own checkbox — check to take the whole category, a dash marks a partial selection — and a one-value group never renders as a group, its value stands at the top level instead (Hotel/Motel, Land), because expanding a row to reveal one row is pure indirection. It replaced a drill (panel-swap behind a back row), which hid the other groups while you browsed one.
  • Transaction type came off the filter bar, 26 Aug [💡 rec] — it briefly sat there pinned to the three values Tony’s Zoho forms fix (Acquisition · Refinance · Construction loan, per his Figma comment #2), then every line of evidence pointed the other way: the matching query never reads transaction_type, six of the eight deal names already carry the word, the shipped My Deals rows don’t print it, and Janover’s board neither shows nor filters it — transaction words live in its free-text deal titles. The vocabulary fix his comment asked for survives where the field still shows: the deal detail’s Transaction fact says Acquisition, not Purchase. Type of Financing — the facet his comment’s three surfaces actually share — holds the filter slot instead. ⚠ Whether transaction type is a concept of its own at all is question 76.
  • Type of Financing joins the filter bar, the table and the cards [💡 rec · comp 26 Aug] — three independent sources elevate the same facet: the matching query scores on type_of_financing and never reads transaction_type; the shipped My Deals rows print it beside city and state; and Janover Pro’s deals board filters by it under the name Execution Types (its bar: Search · Property Types · Execution Types · Footprints), leaving transaction words — “Land Acquisition”, “Leveraged Buyout”, “Sale Leaseback” — to free-text deal titles. The filter carries the canonical 17 with the same type-ahead as Property type (17 also crosses the scan-vs-type threshold); the table adds a Type of Financing column and a sortable Updated column — recency is the one signal the table lacked, and both the live rows and Janover show it; cards get the financing value under the property line. Sample deals carry one financing value each — except Gulf Coast, which carries none, because the shipped request left the optional field blank; the table prints Not specified and the board card drops the fact rather than showing an empty row. The real column is an array.
  • The facet is labeled Execution type, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — every surface that showed Financing or Type of Financing (filter, table column, board card, deal summary fact, form label) now says Execution type. Tanya’s call, and the vocabulary was already converging there: Janover Pro’s board filters it as Execution Types, Tony’s Zoho forms ask Executions to Explore [T], and the live form buries the same dropdown under a Transaction Details heading it shares with the Purchase/Refinance radio — a heading that names neither field. The data key stays type_of_financing; the label is the design decision. Sentence case, 12 Sep (Tanya) — the 28 Aug pass reached the form label, the deal summary fact, the board card and the column-picker entry, and this note claimed it had reached every surface; it had not. The two places a broker reads first — the filter bar trigger and the column header on all four lender tables — still printed Execution Type, and the column picker carried the facet twice, 22 lines apart, cased two ways (COLS title case, FIELDS sentence case). Every neighbour was already sentence case — Loan range, Property type, Loan amount — so the capital T read as a proper noun the vocabulary does not have. All of it is sentence case now, and this record is corrected: the 28 Aug pass was partial.
  • Branch fields under the Transaction segment, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — picking a segment now reveals the branch the live form and Tony’s Zoho §4 both keep: Acquisition — purchase price, under-contract status, target closing date; Refinance — property value, outstanding loan balance; Construction — total project cost, shovel-ready [T]. Two divergences are deliberate: the live form hard-requires Under Contract and Outstanding Balance — here they are soft nudges in the warn panel, keeping creation under a minute; and Construction has fields at all — the live form has no Construction branch. Only the visible branch saves; switching segments discards the other branch’s values, as the live form’s hidden fields do.
  • Overview coaching moved from tooltip to rail, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — the live form hides its best guidance behind a “Tips for a good summary” hover: cash-out purpose, rehab scope/costs/status, refi history, purchase cap-rate and submarket. The same prose now sits in the “Make this deal stronger” rail, keyed to the selected Transaction segment and visible without hovering — Acquisition and Refinance lines carry the tooltip’s wording; the Construction line (budget, timeline, lease-up plan) is composed from Tony’s Zoho construction checklist [T], since the live form has no Construction branch to coach. The tip shows while the overview is empty, then yields the rail to the next gap. Amended 1 Sep (Tanya): the card header regained an info icon — a hover tooltip carrying the same segment lines as a permanent reference, since the rail line leaves once the overview is filled — and the field’s inner “Overview” label came off: the card title already names it, the placeholder carries the prompt, and the textarea keeps an aria-label.
  • Upload dropzone joins the Documents card, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — both intakes have one (the live form’s “Supporting Documents” takes PDF/Word/Excel/images, 10 MB, 10 files max; Janover’s Documents card takes 50 MB multiples), so the prototype now shows the pattern: choose-files button, drag and drop, a removable file list. Simulated honestly — only names are recorded, the files are never read. The checklist chips came off the form the same day — next to a real picker, mark-without-file read as a duplicate upload control (Tanya, on review). The checklist question — what lenders expect vs what the broker has — moves to the deal page, where the packaging phase belongs; the form’s soft nudge now simply counts uploads.
  • Street address and opt-in data points, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — the location card gains an optional street address (Zoho asks Property Address* [T], Janover requires it, the live form never asks); the map stays off the form — even Janover draws it on the OM editor, not at creation. Below location, a Property details card shows Units, Square footage, Year built and Occupancy as four plain fields — Tanya tried and rejected two opt-in variants (chips, then Janover’s add-zone) before settling on always-visible. Units and Year built are hard-required, matching Tony’s Zoho form where Number of Units | NRSF and Year Built carry the asterisk [T]; the units requirement accepts square footage instead, preserving the Zoho pair for CRE deals. The deal page already rendered units, occupancy and year built from seed data — created deals now feed the same facts. A rail tip carries Janover’s nudge verbatim in spirit: data points strengthen the deal.
  • Highlights and Photos land on the deal page, 28 Aug [💡 rec] — Phase 3 opens where Janover keeps both: the packaging surface, not the create form. Highlights sit above the overview prose — Janover’s own copy calls them “the first thing lenders read” — as an editable 3–5 bullet list with an inert Generate with AI affordance; Riverside ships with three sample bullets. Photos take the right rail above the map schematic: hero image and thumbnail strip. Both sections read clean and edit behind a per-section toggle — a first version put inputs, remove buttons and the AI affordance straight into the view, and Tanya called it “too much info and actions”; LinkedIn’s profile (pencil per section), Julienne’s recipe editor and Wix’s per-block dialogs all draw the same line, and Janover’s own cards carry per-section Edit buttons. Now ✎ Edit reveals the highlight input, per-bullet remove and the AI button (or per-photo remove, the + tile and Janover’s 3+-photos nudge), Done puts the section back to read; edit state resets on navigation. Chosen images render as real client-side thumbnails via object URLs — displayed, never uploaded — which is one step more honest than the document dropzone, because a photo’s whole value is visible. Reworked 28 Aug late evening [💡 rec] to the listing-manager convention Turo, Etsy, Zillow and Airbnb all share: a tile grid with drag-to-reorder, the first tile badged Cover (it feeds the deal page’s OM preview card), the add tile inside the grid, and image files droppable straight onto it. The schematic’s caption loses its “neither is collected today” claim: photos now are.
  • Option F: the OM preview card, 28 Aug evening [💡 rec] — Tanya’s screenshots of Janover’s live deal detail settled the layout question: their deal page is a lender-communications workspace, and the package appears only as a compact preview — one photo thumbnail beside the overview text. Six layouts were mocked (assets/photos-layout-options.html); Tanya picked F, Janover’s own answer. The deal summary now shows the overview as that card — cover image left (168×112, first photo; an N photos badge overlays when there are more — the Airbnb/Zillow card convention; clicking opens a lightbox — arrows, counter, Esc/backdrop close) when a photo exists, plain prose when not, zero layout jump — the right rail’s photo hero/strip is gone, and the map shows just the street address the form collects beneath it — a Location caption and a “schematic” disclaimer were tried and cut (Tanya, same evening): the map is self-labeling, and the address line says everything. Photo management stays in the edit form. Amended 29 Aug: Tanya moved the cover out of the overview card and into the rail above the map — option B's placement with F's lightbox and count badge kept; overview is plain prose again. Then the map became a fallback: Janover's deal page shows no map at all (Tanya's screenshot), so the rail showed the cover photo when one existed and the map schematic only when none did — a placeholder that earns its slot, not a fixture. That competition ended 7 Sep (Tanya) [💡 rec · comp 7 Sep] — the map moved to a Location tab, which appears only on a deal whose photos have taken the rail. A Mobbin sweep of listing and property-record products found no product anywhere that treats photo and map as alternatives: Expedia and Navan run the photo large with a small map card beside or beneath the facts, Zillow drops the map far down the overview body, Airbnb sets them side by side, and Navan keeps both at a single photo. The asymmetry is the whole argument — every deal has an address, most have no photos — so one shared slot meant a deal that gained photos silently lost its location. Stacking them in the rail was built first and cut the same hour (Tanya): it is the arrangement the sample supports, but two images down a 250px rail left the card taller than its own facts and read as a column of thumbnails rather than one cover — the sampled products all have a second column to put the map in, and this rail is the second column. A tab was the only slot left that could give the map room, and it is also the tab the market actually has: Location on Mindtrip and Turo, where a photo-less deal keeps the three tabs and the rail map exactly as they shipped 29 Aug. It fills the card’s width as a 220px band, and the schematic’s blocks became percentages when it did — sized in pixels for a rail box, four fixed shapes simply drifted apart in empty grid once the container grew. The same sweep killed the other half of the plan: no sampled product puts photos in a tab, and where a media-adjacent tab exists it is Location (Mindtrip, Turo), never Photos. Tony asked for a Photos tab beside Documents on the 31 Aug call — and, sixty seconds earlier on the same call, for one slot with the broker choosing [T]. The two answers are not the same design, neither was reconciled, and both are now question 86. His 13 Aug ask names them as a pair anyway [T]: “the nice picture, maybe. Satellite view if we don’t have a picture.” The address field itself is Zoho §2 Property Address* [T], not the live form, which collects only State/MSA/Postal; it stays on the map’s hover tip rather than printing beneath, since the Location fact already carries city, state and zip. Highlights came off the page the same evening (Tanya): Janover’s deal page carries no highlights either — bullets live inside the OM editor, and after F the preview card already tells the story; who writes highlights stays an open client question, so the section waits for a real package surface.
  • Form-to-summary correspondence audit, 28 Aug evening [💡 rec] — Tanya asked whether every create/edit section reaches the Deal summary; six breaks found and closed. Square footage, target closing date, shovel-ready and refinance property value were collected but never displayed — now in the size and Transaction facts. Leverage was the reverse, displayed from seeds but never collected — now computed from loan ÷ purchase price (or property value on a refinance) when no seed value exists. Worst: uploaded documents were invisible — the chips and the Documents tab read only the four-item intake checklist, so a deal created with three real uploads claimed “Nothing was attached”; uploads now lead the Documents tab and every document count includes them. The chips row itself then came off the summary (Tanya, minutes later) — it duplicated the tab, and a row of “· none” chips is noise; documents live in the tab alone. The Contacts row went the same way (Tanya, 3 Sep): it printed “You · Dana Reyes, transaction manager” with nothing to click, while the Contacts card two sections down carries the same names with email, phone and an edit path [~]. One logic bug rode along: the units fact was gated on occupancy, so 42 units with occupancy blank rendered nothing.
  • Money fields take full dollars, 29 Aug [💡 rec] — the five amount inputs (loan, purchase price, property value, balance, project cost) drop the invented type-in-millions M convention for $ 4,500,000 with live thousands separators — what Janover’s OM editor, the live form and Zoho all do, and what loan_amount_cents stores. Tanya’s catch: no reference product uses the shorthand, and an M-field invites a 4500000 typo worth $4.5 trillion. State still keeps millions internally; only the input layer converts.
  • Documents became a checklist of slots, 30 Aug [💡 rec] — the Documents tab left the Lenders on this deal card (its tabs mixed lender counts with file counts) for a card of its own: one list where each required document is a named slot — a lender-voice hint on why it’s asked for, filled (filename, date, download) or open (Upload) — under an N of M provided header. The old two-column split (Attached at intake / Not provided) never linked an upload to the requirement it satisfied, so a raw Screenshot….png sat beside an empty “Rent roll” row it might well have been. Uploads matching no slot now land under Additional documents with a File as… action that assigns them — the mapping is metadata only the broker at upload time knows, and every count on the page recomputes when it’s made. Slot anatomy from fintech verification flows (Gusto’s named dropzones, Airwallex’s filled-slot cards, Faire’s per-requirement descriptions); the single grouped list with per-row status is Origin’s documents page. Not provided as a heading died with the split — requirements speak as the lender now. Amended within the hour: the checklist first shipped as its own card below the lenders card, and Tanya moved it into the Deal summary as a second tab (Overview | Documents N of M) — documents describe the deal, so they belong on the deal’s card, not floating after the lender workspace; the tab pill carries the provided count. Upload buttons then came off the view (Tanya, same evening) — the tab shows state, a one-line signpost points at Edit deal, and uploading stays in the form’s dropzone. The tabs themselves became the segmented control (Tanya, from Janover Pro’s My Deals & Lenders | Bank/CU Prospects pill) — the prototype’s existing .seg component, same anatomy: muted track, white active segment. The count came off the segment label (Tanya) and the zero state became a true empty state — centred icon, No documents yet, the four expected documents folded into one lender-voice sentence, a single Upload in Edit deal action — the file-manager convention (Copilot, Grok, ElevenLabs, Dropbox all centre icon + one-liner + explanation + one CTA); the slot checklist appears once at least one document exists. Polish, same evening (Tanya): every row holds one 44px height whether filled or open (the Download button was stretching filled rows), and the signpost text link became the form’s own Choose files button anatomy — an Upload documents outline button, in the checklist footer and the empty state both, linking to Edit deal. Reversed later that evening — Tanya challenged the detour (“is it right pattern to lead into edit view to upload documents?”) and it wasn’t: documents accrue over the deal’s life, and the slot pattern’s point is slot = dropzone (Gusto, Airwallex; Janover uploads on the deal editor page too). The tab is now the live upload surface: each open slot’s Upload button picks a file straight into that slot, a file dropped on the row files itself there, and the footer / empty-state button takes any documents into the list — no form round-trip, no save gate. The edit form’s dropzone stays for intake-time attachment; both are simulated the same way, names recorded, files never read. Upload vocabulary unified, 30 Aug (Tanya): the form’s Choose files / Choose photos became Upload documents / Upload photos — one outcome-named verb across every surface; Choose named the mechanism and only worked inside a dropzone sentence. The lenders card’s own tabs (Matches | Saved lenders) followed the same evening (Tanya) — they were the last underline tab set left on the page, and two tab anatomies inside one scroll read as two mechanisms rather than one. The counts stay on the segments. The underline set’s original reasoning (ui/tabs.tsx is a pill group, but these tabs switch datasets rather than filter one) is kept in the CSS comment where it stood. The open slots themselves came off on 31 Aug (Tanya): the tab lists only documents that exist — filled rows, then Additional documents — and the four dashed placeholder rows, their lender-voice hints, the per-slot Upload buttons and drop-onto-slot all went with them. What survives of the slot idea is the mapping: File as… on an unfiled upload still assigns it to a required document, and the empty state still names the four expected files in one sentence — expectation lives in prose, not in permanent scaffolding rows. Two parties can upload, 31 Aug [T] — Tony, page inventory row 37, 28 Aug: uploading is “both the borrower and the broker”; a broker or an Admin can ask the borrower, and a broker with an off-platform borrower uploads what he receives himself. The research points the same way and had done since 19 Aug — neither broker interviewed uploads anything (insight 5): Dustin works out of Dropbox and DocuHound, Sean sends the borrower a Drive link and the borrower fills it. The product’s direction is the opposite of both. This is not a second button. The moment two parties can upload, who provided this becomes a fact the row has to carry — a sponsor PFS the borrower supplied and one the broker assembled are not the same evidence to a lender — so every filled row gained an uploader (You / M. Adeyinka · borrower), which it could not have carried before because there was only one possible answer. And a document that has been asked for is neither provided nor missing: d.docs is a boolean per slot, so the requested state is a third value it cannot hold. It is drawn as a dashed row — Requested from {lead} · {when} · not yet uploaded, with Remind and a cancel — and Ask the borrower sits beside Upload documents in the footer and the empty state both. Riverside is seeded three-of-four with a mixed uploader split so the column has something to say [~]; the requested row is deliberately left unseeded, because the control is what a reader should land on and one click produces the state. [~] What is drawn is the request; what is not built underneath it is the delivery, and there are two separate holes. There is no borrower to address — the deal carries a sponsor (entity name, lead principal, liquidity, net worth, track record) with no email, no phone and no login — and there is no outbound mail of any kind, which makes this the second unbuilt mailer in this prototype, the first being the lender invitation the add-a-contact form silently sends. Rather than let the screen imply a message left the building, the click’s toast says so. Per-file provenance and the requested state are read-layer work the deal already has shapes for and can ship now; the borrower record and the mailer are one build, and cheaper raised with Chris as one conversation than discovered a row apart. The last native <select> in the prototype went on 31 Aug (Tanya) — File as… was still an OS popup, the one control that had escaped the 31 Aug sweep through the Financing editor, and the only one left anywhere in the file. It is selCtl now, in the form’s own .fld__sel box at btn--xs scale — 24px inside a 44px row, beside the 24px Download button, rather than the 36px the same box takes under a label in a form. [💡 rec] It is the one dropdown here that holds no value: choosing files the upload, which moves the row out of Additional documents and takes the control with it, so there is never a selection to display and no em-dash row to clear one — the placeholder is the entire label, and it reads as the action it is. Its three-line change branch came out with the tag, since applySel’s da: case now does the same assignment through the shared click path, which is also where its keyboard behaviour comes from for free.
  • Financing became the summary’s middle tab, 30 Aug [💡 rec] — Terms requested, Business plan and Sources & uses left the Overview (Tanya: “can we put this into separate tab?”) for a Financing tab between Overview and Documents: the borrower’s ask, the plan behind it and the capital stack are one story — how the deal gets financed — while Overview keeps the facts, prose and rail that identify the deal. The segment showed only when a deal carried one of the blocks at first; once the tab became editable it is always there — + Add stubs are the way in for created deals. Sources & uses opens expanded now: collapse earned its keep when the block crowded the Overview; in its own tab it is the content — the collapse chevron came off entirely (Tanya), leaving the same fixed caption Terms requested and Business plan carry. The shell behind it was deleted on 31 Aug, when Tanya asked whether sections should open collapsed and the answer came back no [💡 rec]: the tab bar is already the disclosure — Overview, Financing and Documents exist so this card is not one long scroll — and hiding a tab’s content behind a second layer, on a tab the broker deliberately opened, hides the reason they opened it. These are three-to-eight-row blocks, so a collapse buys about a hundred pixels and costs a click to learn anything at all; and since most of Tony’s §6 and §7 is optional, a collapsed caption would look the same whether the section is full or empty — and the emptiness is the thing question 77 is about. Two unreferenced functions came out with the answer so the machinery cannot be reached for again by accident. On 30 Aug the tab stopped being display-only (Tanya: “add functionality for this”): every section — Terms requested, Business plan, Sources & uses, and the rail’s Sponsor block — carries a per-section ✎ Edit / Done toggle (the LinkedIn-profile pattern prototyped for Highlights in August), moved to sit beside its caption on 31 Aug (Tanya) — LinkedIn parks the pencil at the section’s far edge, which survives a one-column profile and does not survive a full-width Sources & uses, where the control ends up most of the card away from the heading it belongs to. Then hidden until the section is hovered (Tanya, same hour) — six always-on Edit controls read as six things to do on a card whose job is to be read, and the tab now carries six sections rather than three. The reveal is opacity, not display, so the caption does not shift when the control arrives; the trigger is the whole section rather than its header row, so the affordance appears while the pointer is still travelling toward the content. Three things stay visible regardless, and each is load-bearing rather than defensive: keyboard focus, or the control cannot be reached without a mouse; the mid-edit state, because the button reads Done then and hiding the way out when the pointer wanders is a trap rather than a tidy-up; and every touch device, since a coarse pointer has no hover to reveal it with and would simply lose the ability to edit — the whole rule sits behind hover: hover for that reason, with Zoho §3/§7 vocabularies verbatim as the selects [T], executions as checkboxes, an editable S&U grid (add/remove lines, live-formatted amounts, totals recompute on Done, empty lines hidden from the view) and + Add stubs where a deal has no section yet. Rebuilt on the design system on 31 Aug (Tanya, four passes) — the editor had been drawing its own controls, and every one of them was a private copy of something the file already owned. The checkboxes were bare <input type="checkbox"> being sized by the editor’s own field rule at width:100%; height:32px, so each rendered as a stretched square with its label knocked to the next line; they are now the .chk component every table select-all uses. The dropdowns were native <select>, which opens the operating system’s own list — grey, system font, none of these tokens — which is the exact thing selCtl was written to replace on the status cells; they are now that control, routed through applySel on a new se: key beside the deal draft’s nd:. And the text fields were a 32px bespoke box under an 11.5px caption; they are now .fld / .inp, the same component the create form’s Deal name uses, at 36px under a 13px label. Two surfaces edit the same deal and they were disagreeing about what a form field looks like. The read view gained a fixed label column at the same time: with auto, each section sized its own column to its own longest label, so Terms requested started its values fifteen pixels left of Business plan directly beneath it — there was no value edge to read down a column. Created deals can finally grow a package. Until now this content had no path into a deal except the one-shot Zoho submission; who authors it in production is Q77 in [[stakeholder-questions]]. On 31 Aug the Sponsor block left the rail for this tab (Tanya asked whether it belongs here; it does): Zoho §6 sits between §3 and §7 in the intake form, lenders underwrite the sponsor exactly like the terms and the stack, and Janover keeps sponsor inside the OM rather than in chrome. It renders as a fourth section — and the rail now carries only workflow: status, photos, the lender list. The tab became two columns rather than a grid of pairs, 31 Aug (Tanya, “something went wrong”) — paired cells meant every row was sized by its taller half, so on a deal with no package yet a 32-pixel + Add terms stub was stretched to 211 to match Sponsor’s eight lines and the tab read as broken rather than as empty. Each column now packs its own sections, which also makes the pairing mean something: left is what the deal asks for — Terms requested, then the Business plan behind it — and right is who stands behind it, the Sponsor and then the Property management running the asset. Sources & uses and Strengths & weaknesses stay full-width beneath, since both are themselves two-sided. Three more of Tony’s sections landed 31 Aug [T] after Tanya re-read his two Figma comments against the tab. Property management (Zoho §8) is a restoration, not a new build: it shipped 26 Aug for comment #8 and was lost in the rework above — the mgmt seed object survived on Riverside with no code reading it, while this strip, the stylesheet and two KB notes all went on claiming it rendered. It now sits beside Business plan, which had been holding a two-column row alone, since who runs the asset is the same question as what the plan is. Strengths and Weaknesses / mitigating factors are §11 and §12 of the template Tony named, and the two his forms cannot reduce to a field — everything else on the tab is a fact, and these are the argument made from the facts. They render side by side because the template pairs them by name: a weakness with no mitigant is an unfinished sentence, and a strengths column with nothing opposite it is a pitch. They close the tab rather than open it — the case is made after the terms, the sponsor, the plan and the stack are on the table. Sponsor gained guarantors and credit issues (§6): carve-out signers and the BK / foreclosure / litigation question are what a lender screens before it reads a single line of Terms requested, and the block had been showing only the flattering half of that section. Pearl District carries a disclosed foreclosure so the field is seen doing the job it exists for. [💡 rec] The em dash and None disclosed are deliberately different answers here: unanswered is not the same as clean, and on an underwriting field that distinction is the whole value. Not added, and the omission is a decision [💡 rec]: §5 Property Details in bulk — ground lease, LURA, environmental, deferred maintenance, tenant concentrations, the utilities matrix. They are disclosures for the package, and twelve Yes/No/Unknown rows would bury the six facts that make this card scannable. [~] Also still unanswered: there is no hotel variant, though Tony’s second form is a hotel intake — rooms rather than units, Brand / Flag, ADR, RevPAR, PIP, demand drivers, and an executions list with no agency in it. Renamed Details, 31 Aug call [T] — Tony, reviewing the deal details walkthrough: “change the term financing to details”. Applied 2 Sep (Tanya): the middle tab now reads Details; the internal fin key and the Execution type facet label (28 Aug entry above) are untouched — his rename names this tab, not the facet.
  • Location filter became State, 27 Aug [💡 rec] — the old facet’s values were literal “City, ST” strings scraped off the sample rows, one per deal. Three reasons state is the right grain: the matching query scores geography by state and never reads city; Tony’s intake form asks State* with MSA cut and postal code separate; and the create form leaves city optional, so a city-less deal rendered a “, TX” badge. The facet now carries the canonical 51 with the same type-ahead as Property type. The table’s Location column briefly kept city + state; on 28 Aug it became State too, printing the full state name — the shipped My Deals row does exactly this (State “Florida”, City blank on most rows), and city + postal code are optional, so the list never shows fields a deal may not have. The deal detail keeps the full address — the record view is where optional fields belong.
  • Loan amount joins the filter bar, 31 Aug [T] — the one filter Tony asked for by name on the 26 Aug call, ranked third in his own ordering (State · Property type · Loan amount · Execution type, the last droppable): “a lender asks what else the broker is working on”, and size is one of the first things they screen by. The bar now renders in that ranking. It filters by bucket (Under $1M through $25M+), not a min/max pair [💡 rec] — a deal’s amount is one number, so the screening question is “which size class”, and the audit already showed what free-typed Min/Max bounds do to a list: the likeliest entry hides the right rows. Buckets reuse the MultiSelect anatomy every other facet has, counts and all; the boundaries are sample [~] — nobody has said where broker size classes actually break.
  • The board follows Janover Pro’s Current Deals board [comp Aug 19] — flat grey lanes on a horizontal scroller, a tone dot and count pill in each lane head, a dashed “No deals” placeholder, card anatomy of title › amount › property type › footer (document and saved-lender counts, date), and a kebab menu on the card with Change status as a submenu — Janover’s path for the same edit. Every count on the footer is real: documents from the deal’s checklist, saved lenders from the shortlist, the date from updated. Tokens, radii and control metrics stay LenderPrism’s. One footer element did not survive the copy: Janover’s owner chip (avatar + “You”) came off, 26 Aug — loan_requests has a single belongs_to :user, no assignee or team concept, and a broker sees only their own deals, so the chip would read “You” on every card and carry no information. If team seats ever arrive, it returns as the highest-value element on the card. [💡 rec] The kebab lost a count too (Tanya, 3 Sep): Matches read Matches (5 · 4 accounts), which made it the widest row in the menu and set the panel’s width off a number, so the menu changed shape from card to card. The other three items are bare verbs and the destination states both figures in its own header. [~]
  • Both views are held to one height. [💡 rec] Toggling list ↔ board changed the card's height by roughly 300px, which reads as a page reload rather than a change of representation — the control swaps how the same eleven deals are drawn, so nothing below it should move. Both are now pinned to --view-h, measured off the table's own body at eleven rows: the board fills it and each lane scrolls inside itself, the table scrolls under a stuck header if the set ever grows past eleven. Lane heads stay put and the cards move under them, which is what every board holding a real pipeline does. Released below 767, where a table row is a labelled block and no one constant can hold both shapes.
  • Three deals were added on 26 Aug for the board's shape, not for volume. [💡 rec] Eleven lanes each holding exactly one card is the one distribution a real pipeline never has — work piles up at the front and thins toward the close. Harborview, Magnolia and Foundry (the three already drawn in the Figma Deals table frame) sit at New and Screening, giving 3 · 3 · 1 · 2 · 1 · 0 · 1 · 0 across the eight statuses. Nothing about them is hand-authored beyond the deal record: their match counts (2 · 1 · 4) fall out of the same five-criteria scoring every other deal runs through, and their saved-lender counts are zero because nothing has been shortlisted at those stages. Funded and On Hold stay empty, so the dashed “No deals” placeholder is visible where it belongs.
  • Board Settings is half-sourced. The button and its position come from Janover’s board [comp Aug 19]; the panel’s contents do not — we never saw inside theirs, so column visibility and card fields are conventional board settings [~]. Both act on real data: a hidden column’s deals stay in the pipeline and in every count (the note under the board says so), and each card field maps to a loan_requests column, named in the row’s hover.
  • Deal statuses are eight [💡 rec · 28 Aug] — New · Screening · Outreach · Quoting · Processing · Funded · Dead · On Hold, a collapse of Tony’s own eleven [T · Figma comment, 21 Aug]: Lead | Prospective Deal · Screening, Sizing & Packaging · Review Loan Request Package · Lender/Investor Outreach · Present Quotes to Client · Secure Term Sheet / Application · Engage Lender/Investor · Under App | Processing · Funded & Closed · Dead · On Hold, supplied verbatim in his comment on the Board view frame. The fold: the three packaging steps become Screening, quotes and term sheet become Quoting, lender engagement and underwriting become Processing. Dead and On Hold stay separate, as Tony had them: Dead is terminal and only feeds post-mortem reporting, On Hold is expected back — fusing them would bury recoverable deals among lost ones, the same trap as the retired fused Agency chip. His eleven had replaced the Janover placeholder set demoed 19 Aug. The schema fact stands: db/schema.rb confirms loan_requests has no status column at all, so this is a new column, not a rename.
  • Opportunities is drawn, 8 Sep [C] — sheet rows 1–2: the rail item that has pointed at an undrawn surface since 31 Aug now lands on #/leads as a list and a detail, and the home widget’s inert lever is live. The mechanism is Tony’s, 27 Aug [T]: 24 hours to respond, counting down on screen; borrower identity gated until accept; accept creates the broker’s deal — entering the board at Leads, his own 31 Aug frame — and decline returns it to routing. The countdown and the masked-borrower state are both new design, per his note on the row. The live page was walked 8 Sep: New Deal Opportunities renders two card stacks — Needs your response, Latest matches — with green/red Accept/Decline pairs, no countdown, no received date, no status column and no history, and the rail route 404s. The sheet asks for a list with amount, property type, location, received date, time remaining and status per row, so the cards became a table in the sheet’s own column order. Four calls are ours [💡 rec]: Accept and Decline live only on the detail — the identity gate makes the decision a read-the-record act, and both comparables that pair a verdict with a record (Juicebox’s review panel, Janover’s Deal Inbox) bind it to the full record, not the list row; the live cards’ one-click accept invites taking a deal nobody read. Decline takes a confirm naming what it does — returns it, irreversible, the borrower is not told — because it is the one one-click act here a broker cannot take back; accept confirms nothing, since everything it creates is immediately visible. It became a dialog over the record, later on 8 Sep (Anna) [💡 rec] — it had been a tinted strip at the top of the body, which put the answer above the question: the button that asks sits in the footer, so replying meant travelling back up the record, and on a scrolled record the strip opened off screen entirely. Same words, same two answers, and no × — an alertdialog’s exits are its answers, plus Escape and a scrim click, which both mean Keep reviewing and leave the record open behind them. The second scrim is lighter than the first: .55 over .55 buries the record the question is about, and the dimming is already done. The buttons speak the product’s vocabulary — not the live page’s green/red one-offs, which appear nowhere else in the app. They are library variants only, since 8 Sep (Anna): navy primary Accept, plain outline Decline in the footer because that button opens the confirm rather than declining, and the library’s own destructive variant — solid fill, white label, ported across from the repo where it had never had a caller — on the confirm’s Decline opportunity, the button that actually acts. The red appears once per decision, on the irreversible click [💡 rec]. Expiry is labeled Reassigned, the record’s fate rather than the clock’s. The countdown ticks live and flips a record to Reassigned at zero, so the quiet state is reachable by waiting. Masked identity draws the gate every lead marketplace runs on (Thumbtack, Angi, Zillow Premier Agent) [~]: deal facts open, identity closed until accept, unlocking into the deal’s first contact. It was first drawn as a tinted panel with four hatched bars standing in for the hidden fields; that came out 8 Sep (Anna) and the gate is one line now — Name, company, email and phone unlock the moment you accept — because the bars drew data that does not exist, read as a loading skeleton, and spent a fifth of the dialog to say one sentence. The four field names are the message: they name what accepting buys. All four records are sample [~]; the Dallas one is the widget’s own. Open with Tony [~]: whether a declined opportunity keeps its deal facts readable afterwards (drawn: yes, with identity hidden forever), and what the borrower sees on their side of an accept — the row says nothing about it. The card header names its contents, the badge names its state [💡 rec], 8 Sep: the header read 2 need your response over a table holding four records, so a title counting only the open ones undercounted its own card — the title is now All opportunities and the count is a gold badge beside it, which simply leaves when it reaches zero. An alert around that count was weighed and refused: every row already carries its own countdown and status, so a banner repeating them spends the pattern on a non-event. The destructive strip fires on one condition only — an open record inside the last two hours — and names the soonest deadline, the one thing no single row can show. The record is a dialog over the list, not a page [💡 rec], 8 Sep, after Anna walked the live product: responding is triage — open, read, decide, next — and a dialog keeps the list, its countdowns and the reader's place in it behind the decision. #/leads/:id still opens the record, so it stays linkable and the back button still closes it; only the backdrop and the × close it, because the house modal's close-on-any-click is right for a picker and wrong for a record a broker sits and reads. The verdict moved into the dialog footer with the clock beside it. The live dialog's content is deliberately not copied: it prints the borrower's name and email above its own Accept button, while Tony's 27 Aug row gates identity behind accept — the mask stays, and the divergence is his to settle [~]. Two facts the live dialog carries were missing and are now drawn, 8 Sep: the borrower’s submitted date beside the received one — live prints Assigned… · Submitted… and the gap between them says whether a request is fresh or has been round the houses — and the transaction’s own clock from the intake form’s §4 branch fields [T], a Target Closing Date on an acquisition and a Loan Maturity Date on a refinance, folded into the transaction cell rather than taking a fact each. Live’s Borrower Location is deliberately still missing and the sponsor block deliberately undrawn: both turn on whether the gate covers identification by inference, which is question 87 with Tony [~]. The dialog was tuned on 8 Sep (Anna): the facts grid drops to three across, since a quarter of 700px wrapped the transaction cell to three lines while Year built sat on one; Auto-matched rides the subtitle beside the two dates — it went up to the title first and came back down the same afternoon, and the second call is the right one: a routing fact is provenance, and provenance belongs with the dates rather than in the name of the deal; the gate strip lightens; the section headings go to 14px, level with the fact values they govern and carrying the rank in weight instead — 600 against the values’ 500 is step enough; at 13.5 they were set below their own content, which reads as a caption; the list’s View takes an eye glyph, the row action naming itself twice over; and the footer reads left to right as refuse, time left, take — Decline anchored left in the library’s solid destructive variant, the clock beside the button whose window it counts. While the confirm was a strip the footer pair went disabled [💡 rec], so the red button asking the question was the only live one on screen; the layer’s own scrim does that now, and the attribute came off with the strip. A settled record now draws no footer at all: it held a lone status badge repeating in one word what the note at the top of the body says in a sentence, and what the row behind the dialog already shows in its own Status column — an action bar with no action left to offer. Then it came off entirely, later the same day [💡 rec] — it was hardcoded, so every record carried it and none could lack it, and a badge with one possible value is a page label sitting in a row’s slot. The page header already says the sentence once, where it belongs: Borrower requests routed to you from your territory and areas of focus. Live prints the fact as Auto-matched 04/08/2026, mechanism plus timestamp; the Received date beside it carried the half that varies. Provenance was then moved to where the two values actually mix — the deal an accept creates records its opportunity, and the Deal summary grid carried a Source fact reading Opportunity · accepted {date}, linked back to the record, or Added by you · {date} on a deal the broker entered himself, on the pattern of the lender profile’s own two-valued Source fact. Tanya cut it within the hour: the summary grid holds facts about the asset and the loan — what is being financed, for how much, where — and a record-level fact broke that single subject, opening a second row to answer a question nobody arrives at the Deal summary asking. [~] So the badge is gone and its replacement is gone with it: the routing fact is stated once, in the page header on #/leads, and nowhere on the deal. The deal still carries opp, so the reverse link is one render away wherever it earns a place — the accepted opportunity names its deal and nothing names the opportunity back, which is a real gap and still open. [~] Open with Tony: whether an opportunity can arrive any other way — an admin assigning one by hand. If it can, the badge earns its place back, but with a sibling value and a field behind it rather than a constant. The dialog’s two fact grids became rows, 8 Sep (Anna, with a reference from a live product): label left on a fixed column, value right, one fact per line. Four across became three that afternoon and then this — in 700px even a third of the width wrapped the transaction line while Year built sat on one word, and the eye had to find a new label column on every row. Rows buy what no column count could: every label starts on the same x, so a section reads as one list of questions rather than three parallel ones, and a value gets the whole width, so nothing wraps that fits. It is written as a .facts--rows modifier on the shared component rather than a .mdl--opp override, since any narrow surface can ask for the same layout, and equal specificity keeps the component’s own media rules reachable instead of having to restate every one. Accept says so in the app’s success colour, same hour: the note at the top of an accepted record is a green alert with a tick, on the ink .lbanner--live and the tone-green badges already share. Decline and reassignment stay neutral [💡 rec] — neither is a failure, and a red or amber note would tell a broker they did something wrong by passing on a deal that did not fit. The footer’s ✓ Accepted badge went with the change: the alert says the same thing four lines above, with the date and the deal’s name in it, and the row behind the dialog carries the badge. The gate line draws on the open state alone, same day (Anna: “does it make sense to show borrower section here?”) [💡 rec] — it is an offer, and an offer only reads as one in the present tense, beside the button that takes it. On a declined or reassigned record the same sentence had gone past tense (they stayed hidden), which describes a shut door the note at the top of the body had already reported, and it left the dialog ending on what the broker did not get. Both the heading and the line come off there, so a settled record ends on Year built — deal facts a broker can still read. The permanence of the gate is now implicit rather than stated, which is the one thing the removal costs; it stays part of the open question to Tony about what a declined record keeps. [~] The settled half of the table got an order, same day (Anna: “do we need to add some sorting here?”) — sortable column headers were weighed and refused [💡 rec]: the queue empties itself inside 24 hours, so it never grows into the find-it problem sorting solves, and against a hard deadline soonest-first is not one view among several — a control offering sort by amount lets a broker file a record with forty minutes left below one with twenty hours. A walk of the running product on 28 Aug moved three more values across that line: Riverside is Austin, Texas 78701 at $4,500,000 (not Houston at $12.0M), Northside’s financing type is Agency (Fannie Mae) on an industrial refinance, and Gulf Coast’s financing type is unset — the field is optional on the request form and that request left it blank, which is what the Not specified cell in the table now shows. Riverside’s unit count, purchase price, NOI and Sources & uses were re-scaled to the observed $4.5M loan so the summary cannot contradict its own header [~]; the numbers are still sample, only their magnitude is now anchored. Sponsors, summaries, the seven deals added for volume (Lakeline, Crescent, Pearl, Old Town, and — 26 Aug, for the board’s shape — Harborview, Magnolia, Foundry) and the other twenty-six bankers — including every colleague sharing an account, and the one Prospector-sourced contact at Ironwood — are sample data, invented so the scoring, the filters and the account rollup have something to bite on. Every deal carries a full financing package from 31 Aug (Tanya: “it should be filled for all deals”) — terms, business plan, sponsor disclosures, property management, sources & uses and the strengths/weaknesses pair, on all eleven rather than on Riverside alone, since a demo where ten of eleven deals open on a column of + Add stubs shows the empty state and not the product. [~] All of it is sample, and each package is argued from that deal’s own header so the tab cannot contradict the facts above it: Sources equal Uses to the dollar on all eleven, Senior Debt equals the loan amount, an acquisition leads its Uses with Purchase Price and a refinance with Pay Off Outstanding Balance, executions match the deal’s own Execution type, and every projected NOI lands between a 7.8% and a 14.3% debt yield on the requested loan — the hotel bridge being the wide one, as it should be. The + Add stubs are still the path a newly created deal takes, which is what they were built for. The seeds were then made to cover the vocabulary, 31 Aug (Tanya: “why not all sources represented?”) — the balance rules above say nothing about variety, so the generator reached for the same three lines eleven times: every sample deal had an identical capital stack, and four of Tony’s seven Sources values — Preferred Equity, Mezz Debt, C‑Pace, Institutional GP/LP Equity — were never drawn at all. Uses was already complete at eight of eight. The sample lender network said otherwise: four lenders fund Mezz Debt and two fund Equity (Preferred), Ridgeway Mezzanine doing nothing else, so six lender records offered capital no deal on the board had a slot for. Three deals took a subordinate slice, each where the property type argues for it [~]: Gulf Coast a $600,000 C‑PACE assessment against the PIP and $1.5M of preferred equity (Florida has an active programme, and a hotel PIP is mostly the envelope, HVAC and lighting that PACE exists to fund), Crescent a $1.6M mezzanine piece behind the highest senior LTV here, and Harborview an institutional LP in place of its retail syndication — two answers to the same question, and a student-housing acquisition is where the institutional one gets asked. None of it touches Senior Debt or the Uses side, because subordinate capital replaces equity rather than the loan: totals, debt yields and the loan amounts all stand. Two things follow from it that are design rather than data. Subordinate capital is a weakness as much as a source, so Strengths & weaknesses now carries the intercreditor on Crescent, the PACE assessment ranking ahead of the mortgage on Gulf Coast, and a 10% GP co-invest on Harborview — the section finally arguing rather than restating. And the grid has no order of its own [~]: it is free text, and Tony’s form lists Senior Debt last, so the seeds impose the stack convention instead — senior, assessment, subordinate debt, preferred, institutional common, sponsor common, retail common. If the vocabulary is ever controlled, its order has to be decided with it, or a controlled list rendered in form order prints the stack upside down. The three vocabularies that name these instruments three different ways are recorded as a conflict in [[master-lists]]. The blue observed badge the lender tables carried came off on 31 Aug (Tanya) — provenance stays in the data flags and this strip, off the demo surface.

Every relative value is an unlabeled “Updated N ago” that stamps the lender record’s touch time, never the relationship — and the View results page, the surface closest to a communication inbox, shows no dates at all (“Previously Saved” and “already contacted” both undated). The rule the prototype demonstrates: absolute short dates for records (the deals table’s Updated column), relative time only for activity fresher than two weeks, and every relative value labeled with its verb — Added 2 days ago on a Prospector row, never a bare “2 days ago”, which is the product’s own unlabeled-clock mistake. Past two weeks the question “is this fresh?” has one answer, so the date takes over. Here there are four, their selections collapse behind +N, and the sentence is the one place the whole query stays legible — “Agency (Fannie Mae) lenders lending $25M+ on Multifamily in Texas.” ⚠ What this page does not have: a score.
