It sorted by recency too until 11 Sep [T] — Tony, on this control: “I don’t think we need this option.” Most recently active is the one of the three the record already undercuts: asked the day before what event makes a lender active, he answered “I, as the Admin, must approve them” — a one-time gate at registration, which cannot say anything about this month, and an order computed off it is an order about nothing (question 91). The default is now Institution A–Z, which is his own ask from 5 Aug and still unbuilt in the product: “we probably need to make this alphabetical.” [~] The row sub-line and the profile’s stale-details warning still read that same field and still gloss it two ways; that half of question 91 stays open. Every competitor either scores fit or states the routing rule — the standalone search is a lookup tool, not a match engine, and dressing it as one would put an invented number on the largest table in the product. The moment a lender is taken to a deal — the picker prints per-deal fit — the score appears, because there is now a deal to compute it against. [💡 rec] Row actions are the profile’s own three — Save to a deal, shortlist bookmark, kebab with View profile / Contact / Report — and the save toast learned to name the deal when the deal is not on screen. [~] Also fixed in passing: the rail’s Lenders item now lights on this route and on bare lender profiles, where before no route existed to light it. The header action came off, 6 Sep (Tanya: “do we need ‘create a deal’ here?”) [💡 rec] — no. The header slot signals a page’s own verb — Deals creates, a deal edits, this page searches — and the button only navigated to #/deals/new, a door the Deals header and the home quick actions already own. The one moment lender-browsing genuinely needs deal creation — the Add-to-deal picker with no deal to pick — keeps its own Create a deal in the modal footer, where the gap is discovered. Same duplication the “My shortlist” header chip was removed for, one level up. The Prospector tab got its save door, 6 Sep (Tanya: “should we make in prospector tab page similar to this?”) [💡 rec] — Save to a deal now sits on every directory row, opening the same deal picker the network rows use; the institution lands on the chosen deal’s Saved lenders tab as a Prospector row, with the toast and undo the deal-scoped page already had. This reverses the footer’s old claim that saving “happens from the deal” — ours, not Tony’s, and it contradicted the page’s own subtitle: search it, then take what you find to a deal. The picker’s rows show each deal’s location rather than a fit percentage, because an institution has no criteria to score — the same honesty rule as the tab’s missing score column. What stays different from the deal-scoped page, deliberately: the zip is a plain input rather than a pencil-edit sentence (here it is search input, not a deal fact), and there is no second h1 inside the tab. The Source filter says Prospector, 11 Sep [T] — Tony, commenting on this dropdown: “So ‘source’ has to do with lenders registered in the Lender Funnel vs those found using The Prospector?” The question is its own answer: the filter option read Found by Prism, and it was the last surface in the product still spelling the value out in a phrase nobody says. The row badge, the lender profile’s Source fact and Tony himself all say Prospector — his word, 5 Aug, “which I want to keep because that means to us, that’s how we find them” — and it is the name he gave the directory page on 4 Sep. One concept, one string. The meta line under a sourced banker kept its sentence (found by Prism, not registered) for three more days on the argument that prose about a stage is a different thing from a second label for a value. It came off on 14 Sep (Tanya) and the argument does not survive the screenshot: whatever the sentence was about, it read as the badge’s own tooltip set in body text an inch beneath the badge, on every sourced row of four surfaces, pushing the role and institution it shares the line with. The badge keeps the long form in its title, where a person who wants provenance can go and nobody else pays for it. The other half of his question is settled elsewhere — Lender Funnel is retired as a name [agreed] 14 Aug, so the registered side of this filter is the network, not the funnel. The selection bar came back, 15 Sep (Tanya, asking whether Save to a deal should go into the kebab with the rest) [💡 rec] — no, and the reason it could be asked at all is that this page had nowhere to put its verb except the rows. A checkbox column shipped here 4 Sep and Tanya removed it on the 7th, because it was a seventh column on the widest table in the product serving an action the bookmark already carried in one click. That argument names the bookmark and does not reach this one: Save to a deal off a deal is click, modal, pick a deal, so twelve saves cost twelve modals and a selection collapses them to one — and the shipped Chan Portfolio deal holds 24 saved lenders, so bulk is the real shape of the job. The bar takes the page’s single fill while a selection exists, the rows keep the outline they were given on the 14th, and nothing is hidden. Hiding was the option that lost: the row would have been left with an unlabelled bookmark whose own tooltip reads Save to your shortlist, and with the labelled save gone there would be nothing to stop the icon absorbing the meaning — a broker bookmarking twelve lenders for a deal and finding them on a shortlist instead. [~] The picker learned a second arity for this: a selection has no one fit to rank deals by, and an average across twelve would be the same invented number the matches table’s scoring chrome was stripped for on 31 Aug, so bulk ranks on the deal’s updated date and prints 4 of 7 already on where the single picker prints a percentage. A lead line explained that ranking in the modal body for an hour and Tanya cut it the same morning — the column it described is three rows beneath it printing those very dates, so the paragraph was read before the list could make it unnecessary. [~] Saving skips whoever is already on the deal, one undo restores the lot, and the toast counts what moved rather than what was picked. One thing the bar had to say out loud — the selection outlives the filter, which is the contract the matches and saved bars already keep, so selecting 27 and then typing into the search left 27 selected sitting over four rows with a button under it that would write all 27. Measured 15 Sep, before it shipped. The count now names the gap (· includes 23 the filter is hiding), the same way the saved tab’s bar already qualifies itself when Set outreach cannot reach every row. [~] The sort moved onto the column headers, 15 Sep (Tanya: “can we add sorting to the table headers instead of this separate dropdown?”) [💡 rec] — yes, and this page was the last table in the file still spending a toolbar slot on it: the deals table has sorted from its headers since it was drawn and carries no dropdown at all. The Opportunities pass refused headers on 8 Sep and that refusal is the test this page passes rather than fails — that queue empties inside 24 hours and soonest-first is the one right order, so a sort could only let a broker bury a record with forty minutes left; the network is 27 rows with no deadline and no natural order, which is the ground the deals table earns its headers on. Three of the six columns sort, and only three can. Lender (the old Institution A–Z), Loan range (the old Largest loan first) and Profile updated, which is new [~] — the column arrived 14 Sep and the deals table already sorts its own Updated, so this is an order the page was missing rather than one invented for it, and it is deliberately not the Most recently active option Tony cut on 11 Sep: that one claimed to order on lender activity, which the field cannot speak to (question 91), while this orders on when the record was last edited, the verb the header names. Property type, Execution type and State stay plain because they are multi-value and fitChips() then hides whatever does not fit the column — sorting them would order the table on an array’s first element and then cover it up. One direction per header, no second-click reverse, which is the deals table’s contract and also the honest one here: each label already names its own direction, so a toggle would make half of them lie. Grouping needed no new rule, which was the thing most likely to block this: lenderRows sorts and lenderTable builds its account bands in the order the rows arrive, so one key orders the bands and the bankers inside them and the two axes cannot disagree — measured 15 Sep across all three sorts. The dropdown survives as one thing only: below 767px the table drops its thead for labelled blocks, so the headers and the sort stop existing, and the old control is drawn for that width alone. The deals table has the same hole and no fallback, which is a bug there rather than a precedent. And the move found a dead value — S.lSort had defaulted to "active" since Tony’s 11 Sep cut removed the option that used it. lenderRows falls back to name for an unknown key and the select drew its first option, so the table sorted A–Z and looked correct; nothing pointed at it until no column lit up. [~] State stopped wrapping, 15 Sep (Tanya, screenshot of a seven-state lender stacked one code per line) [💡 rec] — it was the last multi-value column still printing its whole list, and at seven codes it drove a 200px row against its neighbours’ 56. It takes the cap its two neighbours already have, the same .more button on the same data-exp, so one click opens every list in the row and less shuts them together. What it does not take is fitChips: that measures because property and execution names differ wildly in width, so a count cap cannot be a width cap there, while a state is two letters and three of them are the same width on every row — the count is the width, and slice(0, 3) needs no measuring and no resize listener. Three rather than the chips’ two because the codes are short: it shows the whole list for 14 of the 27 rows where a cap of two would show it for 6. Not caused by the checkbox column, which was the first suspect — measured the same day, the full seven-code list needs 188px and the column offers 146 without the checkbox and 141 with it, so the cell was always ~45px short and the 34px only made a standing problem visible. [~] Then the cap turned out not to be what holds the line count (Tanya, an hour later, a cell reading NY · NJ / · CT / +1) — the slice caps the content, but nothing capped the column. Measured across all 27 rows: three codes and the marker take one line at 141px of content, two from 110 down to 60, and three at 58. Between 1180 — where the table starts scrolling on its own min-width — and full width this table squeezes, and with the rail open at a 1240 frame the State column reached 58px, one code per line. It has a 96px floor now (72px of content once padding is paid), which is clear of that cliff and still well under the 141 a wide screen gives it, so nothing changes where nothing was wrong and the squeeze lands on the table’s scrollbar instead — this file’s stated preference for exactly this failure, written for the 26 Aug screenshots. The separator is bound to the code before it with a non-breaking space, so a break can fall after NY · but never before the dot, which is the orphaned · CT in the screenshot; it buys no line count at any width and is only about where the break lands. [💡 rec]
  • The lender profile lands, 4 Sep [T] [💡 rec] — roadmap row 14, which Tony confirmed on 27 August: “the institution as one record with its contacts beneath it, its criteria, and its history with this broker across all deals”, with four actions — view the profile, contact through the platform, add to a deal, save to the shortlist [T · 26 Aug]. Only the roll-up existed. Of the four actions the prototype had one and a half: Save to deal on a row, and Report inaccurate criteria in the kebab. There was no profile at all — no route, no page, no way in — which is awkward given the largest unexplained number in the study is about this exact page: 28 sessions ran a search, 8 opened a lender profile, a 71% drop [doc Aug 19]. A profile that reprints its row earns no opens, so the two things a row cannot carry lead the page instead: the roster in one direction, the history in the other. Two pages, because the data insists. The account band already refuses to roll a credit box up to the institution — a credit box belongs to a person — so the account page cannot print “criteria” without contradicting the table one level up. It prints Coverage across the roster, in a dashed panel that says in words what it is: “This is a span, not a credit box. Sunbelt Agency Group does not lend — its bankers do, on 5 different sets of criteria. No single deal is eligible for the whole range below.” Everything that can only be true of a person is on the person: criteria, territory, the shortlist, the four actions. The two header marks differ on purpose — a person gets a round navy circle with initials, an institution a squared muted tile with a building — because the roll-up’s whole point is that these are different objects, and a broker two clicks deep must be able to tell which one they are standing on. [~] The history is half real. SAVED already records every (deal, lender) pair with its outreach state; reading it across all deals rather than one is the whole feature, and it is free. What it cannot hold is a relationship that closed — SAVED is live deals only — so LHIST supplies those [~], and live rows lead with an Open badge and a link back to the deal while closed rows carry an outcome. This is the item the research names “the best value-to-effort item in the study” [doc Aug 19]: two brokers independently, and Tony from support calls, said no broker can tell which lenders a deal has already gone to. [~] ⚠ The outcome vocabulary is the finding, not the data. Three of the five values are DISPOSITION’s own; Funded and Lost to another lender are not, because both LenderPrism enums stop at Quoted — the same gap the saved-lenders note records. A closed engagement has nowhere to land in the product today, so those two badges carry a no enum marker rather than pretending otherwise. Worth a line to Chris before it ships. Why this matched, spent once. scoreOf runs on every row of the matches table and the number is thrown away there, because a percentage on a table Tony has not seen one on would be inventing a product decision. On a deal-scoped profile it costs nothing: the five criteria print as pass/fail chips with their weights, over the fit figure. Janover prints matched filters as chips on every result row [comp 4 Sep] — but theirs echoes the filters the user just typed, which is why the same county repeats on all fourteen lines; ours states what the engine actually did. Wrangle groups its reasons by weight [mobbin Aug 13], which is what the weight number does here. One deliberate departure from Janover. Its deal picker footer reads “This Originator will be added to the shortlist automatically”, fusing two of Tony’s four actions into one act. Ours does not, in Tony’s own words: the shortlist is “a top 20–25 they’ve worked with” [T · 13 Aug] — a curated list, and auto-writing every contacted lender to it would pass 25 in a week and turn curation into a log. The footer states the omission so nobody reads it as an oversight. [💡 rec] The shortlist is otherwise Tony’s row 19 answer exactly: per broker, not per deal [T · 27 Aug], so it is a plain set on the broker and never touches SAVED; the toast names which of the two lists moved, because Saved already means something else two feet away on the same page. [~] ⚠ Row 19 is one of the three cost-conditional yeses — “not worth building if it is time-consuming” — and still has no estimate. Drawn so there is something to price. Contacting a lender does save them to the deal, because a lender you have pitched is on the deal whether or not you pressed the other button, and leaving them off would make the Saved tab lie about who has seen it. The composer is honest about what it is not. Contact through the platform is one of the four confirmed actions [T · 26 Aug], but the pipe under it is row 33 — Tony’s “yes to both” with the cost deferred to Chris and no estimate — so the footer says so rather than letting a working-looking Send imply a mailer exists. Same reasoning that took the digest clock off the rows. It follows Janover’s order — Send a Deal opens Select a Deal [comp 4 Sep] — because a message to a lender with no deal on it has nothing to say, so a composer opened without a deal in scope asks for one first. The institution with nobody on file is a different object, not an empty table. Opening Comerica’s profile gives no roster, no coverage panel and no criteria — it explains why (it came from the FDIC and NCUA directory, so it can never appear in a scored match list) and offers the one action that moves it, the paid Request a contact with its 7-day refund [T · row 16]. Its history still works: a Prospector save is a relationship event even with nobody to have had it, and the row says Nobody on file in the Banker column. It had one way out of empty until 14 Sep; now it has two. [T] Tony, 9 Sep, pinned on the Prospector drawer: “Add this section just below. Then create banker”, with two screenshots of the shipped product — a Contact Information block offering a paid search and Add Your First Banker, and the Add Banker form behind the second. The paid half we already had; the free half we had nowhere, and it is the half that matters here, because it is the only thing that moves a row the broker already has the answer to. It is also the action the Contacts column was built to raise: a zero there is an institution nobody can reach, and a broker holding the banker’s card should not have to buy one. The count now sums Apollo’s figure with the broker’s own and the hover splits them, because a cell printing 0 beside a row you have just named somebody at is the table arguing with the screen in front of it — and the sort reads the same function, so a row can never print one number and be ordered as another. Departures from his screenshots. His live button reads “Request contact for 1 credit”, and credits were retired on 13 Sep by his own task doc — so the mechanics he specified in August survive word for word (hold, seven days, refund) on the research allowance that replaced them, and the price half of the label could not come across. The verb half should never have been a departure, and stopped being one on 14 Sep (Tanya, asking why the label differed from the reference at all). The button had read Find a contact, itself a rename of an earlier Ask Prism to find a contact, and neither matched the shipped product, which calls this Request Contact — on the page since August and in our own audit since then: “Open a Bank/CU lender from My Deals & Lenders and use Request Contact.” Nothing in the record ever justified the rename. Three reasons it is now Request a contact, and the third is ours rather than his. It is honest about what happens: you ask, a human works, and it can come back empty after seven days — which is a state this file deliberately draws, so a label claiming a result contradicts the screen underneath it. It is the name brokers already use, and the one action that spends money is the worst place in a product to teach a second word. And our own meter already says it: the counter under the button reads 1 research request held and the plan page sells research requests a month, so a button saying Find over a number saying request was one act with two names — the Class 2 failure this audit catalogues elsewhere, committed by us. The retry label moved with it, Search again to Request again, because the second press is the same act as the first. [~] The object word stays in the label rather than shortening to a bare Request: Loan Request is a core object here, so the verb is already spoken for and only the noun tells the two apart. His form has no title field; ours does [💡 rec], because every contact list in this file prints a role under the name and a record that cannot fill it draws a row that reads as broken beside one that can. And his Select Branch is a dropdown, which is the interesting one: a dropdown implies branch records to select from, and this directory carries a branch count and no names, so ours is free text rather than invented branch names. That his form can populate that select is half the answer to question 84, arriving in a screenshot nobody asked it of — the platform holds addressable branch records. What the form cannot do is the thing the screen has to say. Name, email, phone, city, state, branch — not one of them is a lending criterion, so an institution with a banker the broker typed in still cannot appear in a scored match list. Drawing that only in the aftermath would be a trap, so it is said twice, at the two moments it lands: the toast on the way out (“No lending criteria, so it still cannot appear in match results”), and the block on the profile, whose headline changes from No contact person on file to No lending criteria on file — same consequence, different reason, and the paid search is still the only thing that fixes the second. It was said three times for an afternoon; the third was a blue note above the form’s own buttons, and it came off on 14 Sep (Tanya). A warning over the footer of a form the broker has already chosen to fill in is the one place this can be said where it changes nothing: the toast lands on the act and the profile block lands on the record. These records are kept out of NETWORK for the same reason: NETWORK is what matching reads, and a banker who can never score has no business inside it. [~] They are a third kind of contact and the audit’s own distinction has no slot for them — not registered (no digest, no alerting) and not sourced (nobody verified them) — so the provenance is stated as the only true thing about it, added by you. Where that is stated moved on 14 Sep (Tanya, “do we need to show this badge?”): it had been a badge on every row of the table, and a badge that draws on all N rows separates nothing inside a table — what it was marking was the boundary between that table and the roster above it, and a boundary wants one label rather than N. It is a column header now, Contact you added, carrying the tooltip that used to hang off the badge; and it only draws when the roster is there to be told apart from, because on a Prospector account every row in the card is the broker’s own and the strip underneath already names what these records lack. The drawer keeps its own version and deliberately differs: there the two kinds of row are interleaved in one Contacts list with no header between them, so the provenance rides the row — as the subtitle, where a banker the broker typed in has no title to print. That it therefore disappears the moment a title is typed is a real inconsistency and is open. [~] ⚠ Whether they stay the broker’s own or join the shared directory is Chris’s, and it is not cosmetic: shared, one typo pollutes the network for everyone; private, the Apollo count and the roster diverge per broker. The banner’s old second sentence, which sent the broker to the Saved lenders row to press a button, came off the same day — the button is now forty pixels below it. Sentence one gave up a clause a few hours later for the same reason: the section under it became a proper empty state, titled Nobody on file yet inside the dashed box this file already uses for a slot waiting to be filled — the dropzone, the photo tile — and the same box Tony’s reference draws. So the banner stopped saying nobody is on file yet and kept its own job, where the record came from and what follows from it. Until then the section was a sentence and two buttons under a heading, with no title and no edge, which is a section that looks short rather than empty. The form is inline, not a modal. It opened as one for an afternoon and came into the section the same day, which is what the reference does — the panel headed Add Banker sits under his Contact Information heading, where the empty state had been. Two arguments beyond matching him. This section draws inside a drawer, so a modal over it was an overlay stacked on an overlay. And the form is the third state of a region that already draws two: empty and filled. Nothing in the body changed — the shell did, the heading dropped a level because the section heading above it already names the place, and the footer buttons went btn--sm to match everything else inside a drawer section. It replaces whichever tail the surface draws rather than appending below it: leaving the block that explains the empty case on screen underneath a form filling it is the page talking over itself. Escape now closes the form before the drawer, so one press cancels what you are typing rather than taking the whole drawer with it. Two hints came off the fields at the same time (Tanya) — one said the title field is “not on the live form” and one explained why Branch is free text and cited a question number. Both were our arguments for our own decisions, set in body text on a form a broker fills in; the broker has no stake in which fields live has. They are in addBkForm’s header comment, where arguments go, and the placeholders say the rest. The blue note under the fields lost its two explanations for the same reason and kept both consequences: no criteria, and no alerting. And the deal gate came off with it. [T] Without a deal in scope the paid button used to be replaced by a sentence — “Open this institution from a deal to ask Prism to find a contact” — which is the product asking to be operated in a particular order rather than doing the ordering itself, and it is not what Tony’s reference does: his Prospector profile carries both buttons with no deal anywhere near it. The composer had already solved this exact shape, because a message with no deal on it has nothing to say either — it opens the deal picker first [comp 4 Sep · Janover]. So does this, and the pick finishes the whole job: the institution is saved to the deal chosen and the request is held against it in one press. The tier rules moved into holdContact so the two routes cannot drift apart. What the picker has to do is say why it opened — a broker who pressed Request a contact and got a list of deals reads it as the wrong button firing — so its heading and its sentence change with the intent. [💡 rec] The reference fills the paid button and so does this, on both surfaces — but in the drawer that took the fill off Save to a deal two sections up, which had been holding it (Tanya, 14 Sep, asking whether either of these should be primary at all). An empty state with two outline buttons steers nowhere, which is the one job an empty state has, and on this record the choice is not close: an institution with nobody on file cannot do anything until it has somebody, so saving it parks a dead row while the paid search is the only action that moves it — this file’s own words about the same object, one section down. Save to a deal keeps outline weight and its place; a surface claiming two primaries has none. The empty state’s sentence halved at the same time, 34 words to 20 and three lines to two, on the reference’s own one-sentence shape: what it has to say is the two paths and the price of each, and everything else about how the search works is already on the button’s own tooltip. Where the doors are. Every lender name on the page is now a link, and the two grains go to two places: on a grouped matches row the band name opens the institution and the banker name opens the person; flat, the bold company name opens the institution and the contact name in the meta line opens the person. Same on Saved lenders, on the Prospector rows, and in the directory. The row kebab gained the three actions it lacked, above the existing Hide. One guard was needed: the account band toggles on click, so the link inside it had to be excluded or a single click would both navigate and collapse the group it was leaving. [~] Still open, and it is Tony’s own question. He confirmed row 14 and asked back what default grouping means — ours to answer, not his. The answer this build makes: grouping is the axis the lender list stacks on when the broker has not picked one, and the default is the institution, because that is the unit a broker holds a relationship with and it is Tony’s own 14 August ask (“people should roll up to Accounts within the search results”). The switch is what it costs to see the flat list back. One line, and row 14 closes. [💡 rec]

The action stays in the header. The institution carries the website on its identity line, drawer and page, including the one with nobody on file — a bank pulled from the FDIC and NCUA directory has a public site even when it has no named banker. Email is still absent on purpose: Contact opens the in-platform compose, the one place this prototype departs from live. Open: whether a branch’s main line belongs on a Prospector record too. It is public, and it is the number Prism itself dials — but Request a contact sells the named officer, and a main line printed beside that button reads like a free alternative to it. Held back rather than guessed. [~] Tiles became rows the same day [💡 rec · Mobbin] — five layouts were drawn for this section and then checked against twenty CRM contact records: Attio, Twenty, folk, Clay, HubSpot, Apollo, Front, Calendly, Lightfield, Dovetail, Kajabi, Outseta, Loops, Squarespace, Fireflies, Linktree, Deputy. None of them fills a contact detail. The tinted box is reserved everywhere for counts and measured quantities, and fourteen of the twenty draw the same row instead: channel icon, label in a fixed column, then the value. Our tiles had been borrowed from the loan parameters directly above, where an empty slot is the point because it tells the client what the profile expects to hold — and a contact detail is the opposite case, since the broker is here to reach somebody and an empty slot is noise. The verbs moved up rather than onto each row, which is what the first draft proposed: HubSpot, folk, Calendly and Apollo all cluster a record's channel actions in one band under the name and leave the details below as a plain list. The page already did that, keeping Contact in its header, so it was the drawer that was out of step — its Contact button has left the contact card for the action row. The website stayed a link in its own row rather than earning a button, because a domain is its own verb; Attio and HubSpot both print it that way. The empty mobile stopped saying Not on file, which was ours and louder than any of the three conventions actually in use. Twenty's was built first — the field's own name repeated in grey where the value goes — and rejected on sight: it reads as a placeholder inside an editable input, which is what Twenty has, and as a duplication glitch on a read-only row, which is what this is. It prints HubSpot's two dashes. folk's third answer, an invitation to add one, implies a write permission a broker does not have on a lender's record. Copy details is the one verb the action bar gained on both grains [💡 rec]: a number cannot be dialled from a desktop browser, so the honest action is to take the record with you, and copying the block answers it once for both numbers where a per-row Copy would have to ask which. Tony has not been asked about this. Still open, and the larger half: Apollo masks a number it knows exists but has not sold you — (***)***-**** · Mobile · credits with its own purchase button, sitting in the same list as the numbers you do have, while a genuinely absent one reads No phone number available. That is Request a contact from the other end, and it is his call, not ours. [~] Copy details came off the same afternoon it went on [T] — Tony, pinned on the button: “remove this button.” It was ours, a [💡 rec] raised without asking him, so it goes without argument. What it was there for has not gone away: nothing on this record says what a broker does with a phone number on a desktop, where it cannot be dialled. That answer should be his. The empty mobile changed dash in the same pass (Tanya: “why dash is so long?”) — it had been drawn with two em dashes, which was both too heavy beside a 108px label and a plain breach of the UI-copy rule that keeps em dashes out of the interface. It prints two hyphens, which is what HubSpot actually renders and what the convention was read off in the first place. The email address joined the rows, 11 Sep (Tanya: “add with opportunity to copy”) — it had been held out on the argument that Contact opens the in-platform compose, and that argument was already spent, because the office number sits two rows below and is a wider bypass than an address. Three things in the record point the same way: Tony’s own 5 Aug list of what a registered lender types into their profile puts it first (“their contact information, their email, their phone number, their full name”) [T]; Sean named the same gap on 18 Aug, describing a competitor’s profile as carrying phone and email and then “this is something that you can’t really do in LenderPRISM … there’s no contact anywhere”; and every record in the Mobbin set prints the address and keeps a compose action, which are not alternatives. It is not a mailto, deliberately — though the reason first written here was wrong, and is corrected 14 Sep. It said the deal status pipeline only reads outreach that went through the platform, which carried no tag, appears nowhere else in the KB, and describes a mailer that does not exist: the composer’s own footer, four clauses up this same strip, admits the pipe under Contact through the platform is page inventory row 33, unfunded and unestimated, and says so precisely to stop a working-looking Send implying a mailer. The prototype was resting a monetization argument on a capability it refuses to pretend it has one card over. The honest reason is narrower [~]: a mailto hands the thread to Outlook, where the product can neither show it nor capture it, and Contact is the surface that could do either once row 33 is built. A Prospector record prints two hyphens for it, since Tony was explicit that the Prospector holds none of that until an admin’s call produces it. Copy came back as a row affordance rather than a bar button — which is what he struck: a standing labelled control announcing itself beside Save and Contact. On the row it is a quiet icon on the value it copies, and it answers the question the bar button could not, which of the two numbers. The name and the website have none: a name is not copied, and a domain is already its own verb. Office became Direct line, and the name row came off, 11 Sep (Tanya: “I think the number here should be personal number, no?”; “this is the duplicates info”) — two fixes to the same card in one pass. The first label was ambiguous by construction: on a contact who is visibly attached to an institution, Office reads as the institution’s front desk, which is the one number the record deliberately withholds while the branch-main-line question is open with Tony — the label was quietly claiming the thing we chose not to ship. Direct line says whose number it is. Tony’s own 5 Aug wording was already possessive and singular: “their email, their phone number, their full name.” [T] And the Contact person row restated the surface’s own heading — the name is the h1 on the page and the title in the drawer — which is the same duplication the 7 Sep pass struck the whole card for. The card now holds only what the header does not: email, two numbers, the site. The footer sentence became an info icon on the title, 11 Sep (Tanya: “remove this”, then “Add this into the tooltip and info icon near titles”) — as a standing footer, “The lender entered these on their own profile” stated provenance nobody was doubting, under every registered record. Both sentences — that one and the Prospector’s “Prism’s team phoned the branch for this one” — now sit behind the same ⓘ control the Deal overview and Contacts headings already use, on both grains, answering only the reader who asks. The card body is data alone. The note sublabels followed, and the drawer tooltip got its anchor, 11 Sep (Tanya: “I don’t see tooltips, put this in tooltip as well”) — the ⓘ drawn into the drawer heading earlier that day was painting its card off-anchor: .tt positions against the nearest positioned ancestor, which in a card heading is .hd__grp and in the drawer heading was nothing nearer than the drawer itself. The button now anchors itself. And · only visible to you left the Private notes heading for the same control — with · from Prism, visible to every broker moving in step on Admin notes, because the two sections were built to differ in their sublabels and in nothing else, so one migrating alone would have broken the very anatomy that carries the distinction. Both grains. The who-may-read fact now costs a hover, which is the trade the client asked for. The row values dropped from semibold to regular the same day (Tanya: “use regular font here”) — the 600 weight had been carried over from the loan-parameter tiles the rows replaced, where a bold figure against a grey label earns its contrast; four stacked semibold lines read as shouting. Labels already sat at regular grey, so the rows now separate by colour alone. The Mobile row died the same evening (Tanya: “why it's still 2 numbers?”) — the two-slot model rested on the plural in Tony's written comment (“phone numbers AND website link”), but the 8 Sep call transcript holds his verbal as singular (“we should also have, uh, yeah, phone number”) [T], and his pin on the first row read “should be personal number.” Two of three signals say one number, the person's own, so the card carries a single Direct line and the plural stands as the counterweight on record. The curated meeting notes never captured the interjection; only the raw transcript holds it, which is why the two-slot model survived three days. Direct line became Phone with it (Tanya) — that label earned its precision against a Mobile row beneath it; as the only number on the card it was answering a question nobody could ask any more. The page itself went two-column the same evening, 11 Sep (Tanya: “make cards look more compact, but fill the space logically and clear to easy scan content”) [💡 rec · Mobbin] — five layouts were drawn and checked against sixteen record pages (Zoho, folk, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Apollo, HubSpot, Lightfield, Outseta, Attio, Twenty, Zendesk, Front, Plain, Copilot, Wellfound, Nextdoor), and nobody ships full-width stacked cards at desktop width — every record page panes. The winner is the Lightfield/Attio/Front shape: what you read (criteria, notes, deal history, the roster) in the center column, what you look up (contact information, source) in a sticky 340px rail that never scrolls out from under the reader. The rail renders the drawer’s own contact rows at close to their native width, so the two grains finally share one drawing. The staleness banner folded into the rail’s Source card — it is about the contact details and now sits beside them — and the Source fact left the loan-parameters grid for the same card, so nothing states it twice. Last-active stayed in the header sub alone, under the duplication rule. Empty states dropped from ~200px boxes to one-line rows with the action inline, both surfaces — Attio’s “No notes” is ~80px, Twenty prints a grey sentence, and nobody in the set spends dashed air on absence; the dashed border survives as the could-hold-one signal. Two grid traps cost a pass each: grid items default min-width: auto, so the email’s intrinsic width blew the rail card to 525px inside its 340px column, and the main column’s cards overflowed the 900px viewport the same way — both zeroed. The rail’s label column tightened to 70px, since its longest word is “Website.” Below 980px the rail stacks above the main column, contact first, the drawer’s own order. The Source card became the Record card an hour later (Tanya: “this section always contains alert? find more logical layout for it”) — it did not: the banner only printed on a stale profile, so a fresh record showed a bare one-line card and a stale one a card with a siren bolted under a fact. Now the card states the same two facts on every record — Source, and Profile updated — and staleness is the second fact’s value state: gold with the warning triangle when the profile has aged (“1 month ago · contact details may be outdated”), a neutral “This month” when it has not. The heading changed from Source to Record because the first row’s own label is Source, and a heading repeating its first row was the duplication rule again. The card is drawn tinted (Tanya: “like on example”, pointing at the deck’s own mockup, which had drawn the rail’s second panel muted): reference metadata, the rail’s quiet half, not a peer of the contact card. The website link took its own ellipsis with it — text-overflow only dots a block’s own text, and the value is a button, so it was clipping mid-letter at rail width. The main column took a 900px cap and the facts went three-across (Tanya: “make 3 column here, and make these sections narrower”) — on a wide monitor the cards were stretching past 1500px, an admin note floating in a card three times its width; ~90ch at 13px is the reading limit, and the limit should come from the measure, not the window. The fourth facts column was mostly air once Source left for the rail; six facts now fill two clean rows of three. The admin note’s grey box lost its own 76ch cap in the same pass (Tanya: “make the gray background fill the all card width”) — it predated the column cap, and two caps left the box floating in air; the 900px column is the measure now. The account grain took the same shell, 11 Sep (Tanya: “align layout logic for accounts”) — with one departure the grain demands: the roster is the page’s payload and a seven-column table, so it keeps the full shell width, and the two-column split starts below it — coverage and deal history center, a new Institution card in the rail holding the identity facts (type, charter, branches, website) that had been jammed into the header sub line. The header sub reads type and banker count alone now. The nobody-on-file institution keeps the same shape: its Institution card still has all four facts, because a bank pulled from the FDIC and NCUA directory has an identity before it has a banker. The provenance ⓘ came off Contact information, 12 Sep (Tanya: “remove tooltip here”) — the sentence had moved footer → icon the previous day and now leaves the heading entirely, on both grains, since the same pass had put it on both. What it said is not lost: the rail’s Record card states Source as a standing fact on every profile, which is the same claim as a value rather than as a hover, and the Prospector chip rides the title on both surfaces. So the heading was carrying a third telling of something the page already says twice. [~] Still on their headings: the ⓘ over Deal overview, Contacts, and the two note sections — those answer questions their surfaces do not otherwise answer. The Figma drawing caught up, 14 Sep (Tanya: “align this card in Figma with prototype, move values to the left a bit”) — the twelve rail contact cards in the Broker file had been cloned from the drawer and never took the rail’s own override, so five things were off at once. The label column stood at 108 where .lprail .crow .k is 70, which is the whole of the drift that was visible: values sitting 38px right of where the prototype puts them. The copy glyph was pinned at 316, the button’s own left edge rather than the 13px icon the prototype centres in that 26px box at 322.5, so on the rail it collided with the truncated email — the drawer had it right at 544, which is how the error stayed invisible: one grain of the same card was correct. Email truncation had been eyeballed per card, 162 to 195 where the live .v measures 198, and two of the twelve overran the row. Two stacked 1px rectangles drew a doubled rule under Website, which this card does not draw at all: .crow separates with border-top, so the last row has nothing beneath it. And the provenance ⓘ was still on the heading, two days after it came off both grains here — it went from the three drawer sections in the same pass, since removing it from one grain alone is the exact drift the shared contactRows was written to prevent. One divergence left standing, and it is a question for this side rather than for the drawing [~]: Figma draws these rows at a flat 35 to 38px and the prototype measures 44, 45 and 39 — the 26px copy button sets the height of the two rows that carry one, and the website row, which carries none, is the odd five pixels shorter. Three contact rows in a column of three different heights is ours, not Figma’s, and if it is worth fixing the fix belongs in the stylesheet. Tony on the email, 9 Sep, read 14 Sep [T] — pinned on this card: “All contacts should display phone numbers. As for emails, if we are encouraging people to stay on the platform, we probably don’t want to display the email address, but we also don’t want to withhold it. How can we address that?” The first sentence is already built — every record carries a number, the Prospector grain included — and its value is what it rules out: the Apollo pattern logged above as his call, not ours, a credit-masked (***)***-**** with its own purchase button, is out. The number is not a second paywall behind the contact reveal. It leaves the branch main line untouched, since a switchboard is not a contact. The second he answered himself on 26 Aug, and it is not a design question at all: page inventory row 33 reads build platform-send and capture outside sends, and his reply was “I would say ‘yes’ to both” with the mechanism in his own words, a Zoho-style drop address that attaches email to records — cost unknown, deferred to Chris, no estimate [T · 26 Aug]. If an outside send still lands on the deal record, displaying the address costs nothing the platform was going to keep: the goal was never that the broker types into our textarea, only that the outreach is visible on the deal, and capture gets that without asking anyone to abandon their own mail client. So the choice is not hide-or-show, it is whether row 33’s second half is funded — which is question 97, and which is where he parked it five weeks ago. Nothing on the card changed, and two things were deliberately not built [~]: no masking or reveal-on-click, because the contact block already opens behind a per-deal reveal and masking after an unlock charges twice for the same thing — while a copy affordance and ordinary text selection make any mask cosmetic, and withholding recreates the gap Sean named on 18 Aug (“there’s no contact anywhere”) that this card was built to close; and no tooltip claiming outreach is tracked, which would be the row 33 pipe again, asserted in copy instead of built. If capture is ruled out, masking comes back as the least-bad option and should be domain-visible with the local part hidden, so the record still reads complete [💡 rec]. The gate was refusing a broker who had done what it asked, 14 Sep (Tanya: “I can’t see contact info even I’m adding it to the deal”) — on a profile or drawer opened without a deal in scope, the veil printed Open Ruth from a deal’s matches or saved lenders to reveal them and offered no way to do it, while the app knew exactly which deals carried her. That is the defect the empty note log and the empty deal history were both fixed for on 7 Sep — an empty state that names an action should offer it — and it read worse here than a dead end, because the broker who had just saved the lender was being told to go and do the thing they had done. The unscoped branch now reads the same store the rest of the app does: not on a deal states that and stops, because the save is already on the screen and a third copy of it was the next thing to come off (below); on one or more offers Reveal for <deal> per deal, the identical control the scoped surface carries, since the handler keys off dealId:lenderId and never reads the route — the prose was the only thing that had ever separated the two surfaces; on more than three falls back to the sentence. The cap started life as a measurement — the veil had 136px and three buttons needed 155 — and survived the redraw below on the softer ground that past three a stack of strips stops being an answer and becomes a menu. Two further faults surfaced while fixing it, both of which the old prose had been hiding [~]. The reveal caps sat after the scope split, which was harmless only while the unscoped branch offered no button — they now run before it, or a broker with nothing left this month would have been handed a Reveal on the one surface that never checked. And the already-revealed test was keyed on the scoped deal, so spending a reveal from the unscoped surface debited the month and left the veil standing: it now matches any key for this lender, because the per-deal key prices a reveal and does not compartmentalise what the broker has already paid to see. Hiding a contact because somebody walked in through a different door is the same complaint one layer down. Both grains, one function. Then the gate itself was redrawn, same hour (Tanya: “why it 2 steps there? explore how it works in other products … improve ui”) [💡 rec] — the fixed logic was landing in a broken drawing. The block blurred its three values and floated a centred filled button over them, and four screenshots showed what that costs: the veil’s own line was struck through by the row dividers underneath it, the filled button read as a modal dropped onto the card, and Reveal for Old Town Mixed-Use Bridge ran past the 342px rail. The pattern was borrowed from the wrong shelf. Blur-plus-centred-CTA is what Crunchbase Pro, PitchBook and Statista do, and they do it to sell a subscription to somebody who is not a customer yet — the blur is the advertisement. Here the broker is already the customer and the spend is one small per-record action, which is a different problem with a settled answer: Apollo, Lusha, RocketReach, ZoomInfo, Cognism and Hunter all keep the row, mask the value in place, and never blur. So the rows keep their shape and the action left the overlay for a strip in normal flow — which also retires the geometry problem entirely, because the card now grows with the number of deals instead of the veil colliding with them; the two-button ceiling measured earlier that day is gone, and the cap that replaced it is about reading rather than pixels. The mask shows what is already public and hides only what is sold [~]: eight dots and then the real domain, the real area code and then dots. Neither leaks — the institution card prints that same domain ungated and the area code is derived from the lender’s own first state, which the header names — and the dots are fixed at eight rather than one per character so the mask does not give away the length. The website stopped being gated at all, which the blur had been doing: a public domain that the institution card already prints is not a paid contact detail, so hiding it bought nothing and cost the locked card its only readable row. And the redrawing quietly answers half of Tony’s 9 Sep question from the other side: a masked row that shows the domain states the record is complete while withholding the part you pay for, which is exactly the “we don’t want to withhold it” constraint he could not see a way to meet. Why it is still two steps, and why that stays — saving a lender to a deal is free and reversible, unlocking their contact spends a reveal from a monthly cap, and collapsing them would make every save spend one. The two steps only appear on the path where the lender is not on a deal yet; once they are, it is a single click. What was wrong was that both steps looked identical, so the first one read as having done nothing. Not taken [~]: a combined Save and unlock that does both from the picker. It is the better single gesture for somebody who came to this card wanting the contact, but it spends a capped resource from inside a picker built for a free action, and the header already carries a save-only button two inches above. Worth raising with the monetization screens rather than slipping in. And the strip’s own Save came off half an hour later (Tanya: “now ‘save to deal’ action is duplication”) — it was the second copy of that button on each grain. The drawer already carries Save to a deal as the record’s primary in its action bar, and the page carries it inside the empty Deal history state under the 7 Sep rule that an empty state naming an action should offer it. Both of those are earned: one is the record’s own action bar, the other is the section actually about deals. The gate’s job is narrower — say why the values are masked, and offer the unlock — and with no deal there is no unlock to offer yet, so it now states the condition and stops. Noted while counting them [~]: the two grains disagree about this button. The drawer’s action bar has it; the page’s carries only Contact and Save to shortlist, so on the page the save lives only inside the Deal history empty state. That is a breach of the same align-both-grains rule this card was rebuilt under on 7 Sep, and it is older than anything in this pass — left alone rather than widened into. The drawer’s section icons came off, 14 Sep (Tanya: “remove icons near all these titles”) — eleven of them across both grains: Loan parameters, Property types financed, Execution types, Territory, Contact information, Private notes, Admin notes on the banker, and Coverage across the roster, Contacts, About this institution, Contact information on the account. They arrived on 7 Sep from live, redrawn out of its emoji into this file’s own line strokes — and the very same pass had already refused to put them on the profile page’s cards, on the grounds that page cards match the rest of the app, not the drawer. So the drawer had been left as the only surface in the product whose section headings wore one, which made the icon a fact about which panel you were in rather than about the content. And they were decorative in every case [~]: a dollar sign over Loan parameters, an envelope over Contact information, a building over Property types financed — each restating the word underneath it, which is the same duplication test that took the Contact person row and the Source heading off this card. Taking them off settles the divergence in the direction the rest of the app had already gone, rather than propagating it. The ⓘ buttons stay on Private notes and Admin notes: those carry the who-may-read-this fact the heading cannot, which is exactly why they were moved there on 11 Sep. Figma still draws them and is now out of step on this one [~]. The two stateless gate lines took the opportunity note’s anatomy, 14 Sep (Tanya, pointing at the borrower gate: “use this ui with one line text”) — the no-deal and many-deals states had been drawn as a bold line over a muted one with a bare lock beside them, which is the anatomy of a row, and neither of them is one: there is nothing to act on, so there is nothing for a row to carry. They are now .oppnote, the same tinted panel the opportunity dialog uses for Name, company, email and phone unlock the moment you accept — borrowed whole rather than copied, with a margin modifier as the only difference, since a private reimplementation of a component this file already owns is the trap the editor’s own controls fell into on 31 Aug. One line had to be made to mean one line: the rail gives the sentence 287px and the first draft, which named the fields the way its source does, measured 350 and wrapped to two. Naming them is right in the opportunity dialog because the fields are the message — nothing on that record shows them — and wrong here, where the masked rows sit directly above the panel already labelled Email and Phone. So the sentence carries only the trigger, and it is cut against the longest first name in the network rather than against the one on screen. The states that can act keep the row: a tinted panel states a fact, a strip offers a verb, and the deals a broker can unlock on are a list of verbs. [~] Then the gate moved above the rows and the caption came off, same hour (Tanya: “remove this text; place this section below the Contact information title”) — both halves of one correction. Contact details unlock per deal had been narrating what the control underneath it already showed: a lock, a deal name, and a button reading Unlock. The sentence was doing a job only because the gate sat at the bottom of the card, four rows below the heading, where it had to announce itself — a broker met three masked values first and learned why afterwards. With the gate directly under the heading the order is the honest one: why it is locked, then the thing that is locked. The sentence has nothing left to do and goes. What survives is the half no control can show — 2 of 3 reveals left this month — and only on Essential, the one tier with a budget small enough to be worth counting. The CSS followed rather than led: the strip’s separation flipped from a top border to bottom padding, and the tinted panel lost the divider that would have sat directly under its own border. [~]
  • Admin notes, 11 Sep [T] — Tony, pinned under Private notes in the quick view drawer: “Just below private notes, we should have a space for Admin Notes.” The third voice on a lender record, and the one the shipped product confuses with the broker’s own. He has raised that muddle three times: on the 5 Aug walkthrough (“these are notes that I, as the admin, put about the lender that… everybody on the platform should be able to see”, against “notes private to the broker”), at the 6 Aug kickoff (“the distinction is not visually clear”), and in design-scope, where clarifying the two is still an unticked item. The audit found live’s version rendering as a badge on the lender row [doc Aug 19], which is how a paragraph of intelligence ends up compressed into a dot. The two sections now differ in exactly the way they mean, and in no other: identical anatomy, opposite sublabels. Private notes wears a lock and only visible to you; this wears a clipboard and from Prism, visible to every broker. Who wrote it and who may read it is the entire distinction, so it is the only thing that changes between them. Both grains carry it, drawer and page, under the rule that already put the note log on both. Neither paint already spoken for [💡 rec] — gold warns about data trust, blue explains record state, and an admin note is editorial content rather than either; it takes a neutral card with a navy left rule, the platform’s own voice marked without outranking the lender’s stated criteria beside it. One staleness signal, not two — his mockup put This information is likely outdated in a box of its own, below a header that already carries the gold Profile last updated N months ago. Two warnings in different words teach a broker to read neither, and they are not even the same clock: one stamps the lender’s last edit, the other the admin’s. The age survives as a gold clause on the attribution line (Written by Tony Talamas, 12 Jun · 3 months old), absolute date past two weeks per the one-clock rule, and Lena carries a three-month-old note on a freshly edited profile so the two clocks are on screen disagreeing. It renders only where a note exists [~] — five of twenty-seven carry one, and a heading promising internal intelligence over an empty box on the other twenty-two advertises a shortage rather than a channel. What it holds is what the fields cannot: a credit committee that moved to fortnightly, a desk that changed hands in April, an allocation close to fully committed. His mockup held the opposite and it is the one thing this must not carry — Homebuilder Finance, SFR Portfolio Loans, 5-50 Unit Multifamily are property and execution types, already structured on the record and already scored by the matcher, so a prose copy of them is a second appetite nobody reads and nothing scores. His own 5 Aug words describe the first kind; the image shows the second. The build follows the words, and the conflict is a question back to him. [~] Three more open [~]: whether it is Notes (his comment) or Comments (his image); whether an institution with no named banker can carry one, since his pin was on a person and nothing in the data model says; and whether a broker who knows a note is wrong has any road to say so, which the word Comments implies and nothing here offers. Notes are given, not authored — this prototype has no admin surface. [~]
  • Executions joined Areas of focus, 12 Sep [T] — Tony, pinned on the broker profile’s Areas of focus: “We should add Executions which is currently our list of Transaction Details in our existing forms.” He is right, and it is his own rule — [[design-scope]] records property types and transaction execution types coming from a single master list used identically everywhere [T], and this section shipped half of it. The broker was the only object in the file with no execution dimension: a lender record carries them (pills on the drawer and the profile), a deal carries one, the broker carried none. Built against FINANCING_TYPES, the canonical 17 the filters, the deal form and the lender pills already run on — not the 9 on his Zoho form, which fuses Fannie and Freddie into one value; the screenshot attached to his comment is that same 17, so the list he pointed at is the list we were already using. Same anatomy as the property field directly above it, a separate store, and the field is a tenth item on the completion meter. Both labels are the facet names, 13 Sep (Tanya, pointing at the two filter triggers) [💡 rec] — Property type and Execution type, exactly as the filter bars, the table columns and the deal summary print them. They had been drawn as Property types you finance and Executions you place, which was a drift from a decision already on the record: [[master-lists]] fixes Execution type for every user-facing surface and names form label among them. The verb problem goes with it — you finance is the lender’s verb on a broker’s profile, and the facet name has no verb to get wrong. And both carry *, 13 Sep (Tanya: “should both fields be required?”) [💡 rec]: the two are one answer split in half — what you finance and how you place it — and the consequence of leaving either blank is identical, a broker the directory cannot put in front of that search. Loan size and geography bound that answer; these two are it. The completion meter had already been counting both as missing while only one wore an asterisk. [~] Worth a line to Tony, since his only recorded word on this facet points the other way: 26 Aug, on the deal search, he asked for execution type to stay optional “for a broader search”. That is the opposite object with the opposite goal — on a deal, blank means search wide; on a profile, blank means be found by nobody — so it does not transfer, but he should be the one to say so. Nothing gates Save either way; the asterisk states what the field is for, and the meter is what actually counts. The real work was the duplication. Three strings live in both vocabularies — Build to Rent, Build to Sell Single-Family & Condos, Note Purchase Financing — so stacking the two lists as adjacent fields on one card means the same chip renders twice, forty pixels apart, by design. Tanya asked on the deal form 26 Aug whether they should simply leave the property list; Tony said keep them (“I believe they are used to match lenders… Removing them could cause issues”) [T · 27 Aug] and Christian confirmed (“That’s correct! Lets not remove them”) [C · 3 Sep]. The reason is migration rather than taxonomy — lender records declare these values on the property side and would stop matching — and nobody disputed that they are financing structures. So the duplication is ratified and the design has to disambiguate rather than deduplicate: the executions list gained its own six groups (ours [💡 rec], the client has never grouped it), so a shared value never appears under the same heading twice, and a hint names the three outright and says the two answers are independent. The groups are derived, not typed: FINANCING_TYPES is now flattened and sorted out of FINANCING_GROUPS and reproduces the previous array byte for byte, so the filters are untouched and the two cannot drift; the shared-value list is computed against PROPERTY_TYPES rather than hardcoded, so the hint stays true if either list moves. Still open, and neither blocks the field [~]: his pin names Transaction Details, which is a section heading over two fields on the live form — the financing multiselect and the Purchase/Refinance radio — so whether he also wants a transaction dimension here is unanswered, and that is question 76 part 3. And what this field does is undecided: Areas of focus feeds directory search and possibly opportunity routing, never lender matching, so executions here change who finds the broker rather than match quality — Q33 again, from a second direction. One thing his comment settles for free: the Execution type label was Tanya’s call on 28 Aug and was never raised with him; he used the word himself, unprompted.
  • Both Areas of focus vocabularies became the multiselect, 12 Sep (Tanya: “is it better to use multiselect dropdowns for both Property type and Execution type?”) [💡 rec] — yes, and the chip grids came off the same hour they were completed. Chips were never a recorded decision here: they date from the first-session prototype when the property list was eight values, and survived it growing to twenty-four. The argument is the steady state. A filter is set and read once; a profile field is written once and read for the life of the account. The two grids cost 1030 pixels and forty-one chips to express eight facts — the answer roughly a tenth of the pixels, and the loan range and states pushed under the fold — so the grid was optimising the single sitting a broker does and taxing every reading after it. The card also disagreed with itself: four fields, three idioms, and the field that was already a multiselect was States, the longest vocabulary on the card at fifty-one. Nothing new was built. msCtl was lifted out of the filter bar on 3 Sep expressly so a form field could use it — its own comment says so, and the States field is the proof — and the grouped accordion is already how both filter bars pick these two lists. Two MSX descriptors, and the one-value-group rule folds Hospitality and Land to the top level for free. The overflow pattern was argued one way and settled the other. These two fields first got a ms--wrap modifier so the trigger stated the whole answer, on the reasoning that a filter collapses overflow into +3 because its selection is transient while a profile’s is the record. Tanya’s call, 13 Sep: use the filter’s pattern here too — same control, same vocabularies, and the States field beside them had never wrapped, so the card was carrying two overflow idioms to avoid one truncation. The modifier is gone and all three fields behave identically: fit to one row, ellipsise the first badge when even it does not fit, count the rest. [💡 rec] What it costs is not hidden here — a broker cannot read their own full claim off a closed trigger, and reopening the control is the only way to see it. It also dissolved the duplication problem the entry above was built to solve, and then the treatment with it: two collapsed controls never show Build to Rent twice on one screen, so the explanatory hint was removed outright (Tanya: “do we need to show this text?”) [💡 rec]. It had been written for two open chip grids putting the same chip on screen forty pixels apart; that moment no longer happens, and the group headings carry the rest — Multifamily & residential against Construction & development. Three things were wrong with keeping it: it explained the data model rather than the broker’s decision (a lender can be matched on either answers a question nobody on this screen asked), it was the longest text on a card of four short fields and sat between them, breaking the two-column rhythm, and the reasoning was design rationale rendered as user copy — it already lives in this strip, the code comment and [[master-lists]]. SHARED_TYPE_VALUES went with it, having existed only to keep that sentence true. And it surfaced a real bug [~]: the group select-all checkbox resolved its control by group name through FILTERS, so with three controls now sharing PROPERTY_GROUPS the first match won — the lender page’s select-all had been writing into the deals filter’s set all along, and the profile field would have been the third casualty (executions would have thrown outright, since no filter declares those groups). It now resolves through the data-msg on the control the click is inside, and calls sync like the other three paths. The dead .pchip / .pgrp rules and both toggle handlers came out with the grids. Then the pair went into one two-column row (Tanya, pointing at the min/max loan row: “make same layout as here”) — Property types and Executions now sit side by side in a .fldrow--2, over the loan range and States, so the card reads as two columns down to the field that has no partner. Card 1228px → 344px from where the chip grids left it. Two things had to be fixed for the row to hold. The shared-value hint left the executions column for a row-spanning one, since it was a fact about the pair rather than about either field — and was then dropped altogether, below. And while the triggers still wrapped, the two ended at different heights — four property types took two rows, four executions three — which surfaced a rule worth keeping after the wrapping went: .fld:last-child { margin-bottom: 0 } was defeating the grid’s own stretch, because in a two-column row the last child is a neighbour, not the bottom of the stack, so the right-hand field was quietly claiming 16px more usable height than the one beside it. Both columns carry the margin now. It is invisible while every control in the row is a fixed 37px and it is left in place deliberately: the next row that holds anything content-sized would hit it again. [~] The Figma frame has no grid, so the shorter box is set to the taller oneexplicitly; token widths there run one to four pixels wider than the browser’s (Inter’s Figma metrics) and are computed from the hugged text rather than copied, so the wrap points still land in the same places.

It is a dialog now, and it does the four jobs a Mobbin sweep of six human-work promises says a confirmation owes [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep]: the channel (email, not a download — a person makes it), the trigger (the moment it is ready), the bound, and a handle. Not one of the six — Dropbox Dash, Plain, HubSpot, Apollo, Workable, Shopify — lets such a promise expire: Dropbox replaces its button with the greyed words Request submitted and opens a history row reading Pending, Plain emails an Order ID to chase with, HubSpot answers in a dialog naming the team and the inbox. And X became a range — 2–3 business days, up to 5 — because both products that state a real delivery window state a range with a ceiling (Plain 3–5… may take up to 7, Dropbox up to 30 days), and one number is the shape of promise a human queue breaks in its first busy week. So the ask to Tony is not what is X but what the range is and what the worst case is. Still missing, stated not invented [~]: there is no delivered state — the memo goes on its way and stays there; no brief, though a memo branded to your firm needs to know which firm; and whether the tier gate is even the right gate, since question 93 records execution support gated on deals over $5M rather than on a plan. The Escape key closes all six monetization dialogs as of the same day — a gap this file had flagged and left open, impossible to leave once a seventh arrived), Opportunities teaser (real rows blurred, real count over them; the trial keeps the full surface so the drawn flow stays demoable — whether a trial previews Pro surfaces is an open question [~]. Rebuilt 16 Sep against twenty gated surfaces on Mobbin [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep]: the offer had been set on the blur, with no ground of its own — 14px bold over blurred 13.5px — and that is the one shape none of the twenty use. Eighteen of them empty the page and centre a card on it; the two that keep the real page behind the gate, Juicebox and Vercel, both float an opaque card over it, which is what the veil holds now, in .mdl’s own floating register rather than a third one. The nav item is where the gate is reached; the page is where it is drawn. Worth one line with Chris, since the doc says otherwise. The blurred half is inert as well as aria-hidden: pointer-events: none stops the mouse and nothing else, so with real rows behind it a tab press walked focus into eight links a broker cannot have. Still Chris’s: the lead assignment rules, which the doc marks TBD and nothing here invents). Not the doc’s word: research turnaround is not TBD — Tony answered 7 days on 27 Aug and the rows already drew it. The cap notice was rebuilt 16 Sep against twenty-eight metered allowances on Mobbin [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep]. It had been a <div class="hint">, and .hint has nine rules in this file with every one scoped to some other ancestor — none reaching /lenders. Measured live: zero matching rules, 14px, no ground, no border, 1306px wide. A full-bleed line of gold body copy, which is why its colour and margin were hand-inlined; the compensation is always the tell, and this is the third instance after .msg and .why. It is an .alert--warning now, the component built 14 Sep whose own notes say both our banners need the dismiss column it ships with. Two edits to that component came out of the same banner [Tanya, 16 Sep]. It lost its 1120px measure: a readable-prose cap on a component that turned out to carry no prose, and measured against all four surfaces that hold a page-level alert — /lenders, the profile, the read-only deal, home — every one sits in .page, whose every other child is 1332 at a 1642 viewport. The banner was the only block on those pages not reaching the edge of the thing it describes, and a short line above a full-width one reads as a different column rather than a shorter one. .home had already overridden the cap to none on the 14th for the same reason, which is the tell: a default that two of six callers opt out of is the wrong default. The narrow callers never felt it — the create-deal footer is 784 and .empty keeps its own 52ch — so removing it moved exactly the four that were wrong. And the title and description closed up, twice over. A grid row is as tall as its tallest item, so the 24px dismiss × made row one 24 and dropped the description 9.2px below the title, which reads as two paragraphs rather than one block; the × spans both rows now instead, align-self: start holding it at the same y, guarded by :has(.alert__desc) so the title-only profile banner keeps the height that 24 box is meant to give it. That left 4, and 4 turned out to be one gap declared twice — a row-gap: 2px on the grid and a margin-top: 2px on the description, adding rather than agreeing. The margin is gone [Tanya: “change to 2px”] and the row-gap is now the only place the number lives, which is the point: a spacing that resolves to double what any one rule says survives review because the result looks deliberate. Both faces compute the same 64.97 as a result, so the band does not change height when a broker crosses the cap and the page beneath it does not jump. The two rows were briefly one [16 Sep] — the description nested inside the title, running on after an em dash, the whole line at one weight, the row centred — and put back the same day (Tanya). Recorded because the round trip paid for itself three times over and every repair it turned up is still in the file. The doubled row-gap: the space between the two lines was 4px and no rule said 4, a row-gap: 2px on the grid and a margin-top: 2px on the description adding rather than agreeing — a spacing that resolves to double what any single rule states survives review precisely because the result looks deliberate. The row-span rules, which now test for a direct child (:has(> .alert__desc)) instead of a descendant, so they stay honest about how many rows there actually are. And the reminder that align-items: start is a first-line rule, not a default: it is exactly right while the prose wraps and exactly wrong the moment a band collapses to one row, where it leaves the text pinned to the top of a row the × or the button is sizing. Two rows is the layout the component was drawn for and the one every other banner in the file uses; the run-on rules are gone rather than left unexercised, since an alert layout with no caller is one that rots. The dismiss centres on the block [Tanya, 16 Sep] rather than sitting on the title’s row, which is the placement .alert__act--end already took: the two share the third column and never appear on the same face, so a control that sat 12px higher or lower depending on which face was showing would be the one thing in the band that moved between them. Both now land on 32.48 of 64.97. The span is what makes it possible — it lifts the 24px box out of row one’s height, so the block it centres against is the prose rather than the prose plus its own overhang. The base rule keeps align-self: start for the title-only profile banner, where one row makes start and centre the same y anyway. It carries no meter, and a first pass gave it one — corrected the same day when Tanya asked whether the bar should be full width and the honest answer turned out to be neither width [16 Sep].
