Every bar that does exist sits in a card 290–460px wide and spans it — which is what .dcap does too, since its 132px is not a short bar but the full width of its header slot. So the rule is a meter fills its container, and a page-wide banner is not a container any of them would put one in; the 260px first drawn here had no precedent in either direction. Two facts close it: the count already states the proportion in words, and the rail’s plan card is drawing its own meter whenever this banner is up, both being gated on revPct() >= 80. A third drawing of one number is not quiet, and quiet is the doc’s own word for this notice. It dismisses at 80% and does not at 100%, the sweep’s clearest rule: Emergent’s running low on credits strip takes an × and its exhausted-credits message does not, and Rox, HubSpot Breeze and Claude’s own usage notice are all undismissable. A warning you can act on later is dismissible; a wall is not. And it has a 100% face at all, which is a hole rather than a refinement: the old banner stopped at revPct() < 100, so at the cap this page said nothing — no limit reached, no reveals used, no alert in the view — and the broker met the wall only by opening a contact. Every product in the sweep that puts a limit on a working surface puts it there at exhaustion, HubSpot Breeze nearest of all: contact enrichment, metered by credits, with the notice and the locked control on one screen. And the reset date was three literals that disagreed [~] — 1 Oct on the banner, Oct 3 on the plan page, in 6 days on the gate, no two of which can be true of one allowance. The plan page had already settled which boundary applies (a paid tier turns over with the billing period; Essential, having none, turns over on the calendar month) but the decision sat in a local const where nothing could reach it, so screen 12 — paid plans only — was printing Essential’s date on the one surface Essential never sees. Lifted to allowResetOn()/allowResetIn(), named for the allowance rather than the reveal cap because the research modal had the identical bug. Both stay .tbd: the doc fixes neither the cap number nor the reset day. Two doors the sweep has and this does not [~]: a top-up for reveals — HubSpot’s “Need it sooner? Purchase credits”, Framer’s Buy Add-on, and this file’s own PLAN.packs, which exists for research and not for reveals — and an escape hatch in Maze’s shape (“Or archive a project”). Neither is invented here; both are questions for Chris alongside the cap number. Worth one more line with him: the doc says “reveal button state” and ours replaces the whole contact block with a panel, where HubSpot does both at once — panel above, padlocked button below). Those seeds paired each paid tier with one heat — Accelerator always over 80%, Pro always under — which read as though the gold meter belonged to Accelerator and the bare card to Pro. The zero is what does the work — every cap surface in this file is written as revPct() >= 80 or >= 100, so an uncapped tier falls out of the plan-card meter, the /lenders banner and the reveal gate without one tier test being added. Tony said this in the margin nobody was reading [~] — the branded memo and the public listing are Pro-only in this file already, and both arrived through his Figma comments in September; he made the same two corrections in the Drive document, where they sat unread for a week alongside this one. The row is Fixed: “Deal details, status → Closed · celebrate + annual offer on monthly plans”. The status it names does not exist — Tony’s eleven collapsed to eight on 28 Aug and Funded & Closed became Funded — so the trigger is Funded and the copy says funded; one line to him, since the doc’s author and the status list are the same person a fortnight apart [~]. The trigger covered one of three paths. S.status[id] was written in three places and screen 14 sat on one, the select that serves the deal page and the table row; the card menu’s Change status submenu and the board’s drop handler both assigned directly, so the two gestures a broker is most likely to close a deal with fired nothing. Dragging the card onto the won lane is the canonical close on a sales board — Pipedrive turns the foot of the board into a drop strip the moment a card lifts, with WON a green target [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep]; ours had the lane and no listener. One setStatus() now, all three writers through it. Essential was offered a discount on nothing — the test was monthly and not trial, which is true of a $0 plan, so tiers carry an annual price and Essential deliberately has none. “First closed deal” had lost its first [~] — Overview v1.2 offers annual on the first deal marked Closed and this reopened the pitch on every close, so a broker who funds four deals in a quarter met the same modal four times. The celebration still fires every time; the ask is once, decided at the trigger rather than in the renderer — computing it at render time set the flag on the first pass and pulled the offer out from under the broker on the second. And the offer led, where twenty shipped celebrations say it should not. A Mobbin sweep of milestone screens found not one that sells: incident.io, Trello, Eventbrite, Zillow, HubSpot, Workable and Vercel all hand the user back to the product; Wave — a finished piece of financial work, the closest analogue — offers Reconcile other accounts, the same job again; Monarch and Uxcel put the figures achieved in the celebration rather than an adjective. Every upgrade-flavoured one (Magnific, Mural, Amie, Figma, Emergent) celebrates a payment that already happened. The single product that both celebrates and asks is Higgsfield, with a ten-minute countdown on 54% off, and it reads as the bait question 94 fears. So the celebration is the header and stands without the offer, the offer is one subordinate row in the body — res0Modal’s own grammar — and the filled footer button is Back to the deal, a deliberate departure from Motion, which gives the identical offer the primary because it draws it on a billing page where switching is the errand [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep]. The second line carries a fact rather than a mood, following Monarch and Uxcel: the amount, the place, and the one consequence true of this account. On Essential that is load-bearing — activeDeals() excludes Funded, so closing a deal is literally what frees the one slot the free tier has, and a broker at the cap who funds a deal has just earned the thing screen 8’s gate was refusing them with nothing telling them. The 🎉 in the heading went with it: it was the only emoji in the product UI, and four of the sweep’s celebrations (Qatalog, Uxcel, Monarch, Zillow) open with a filled green disc and a tick, which is the portable half of what the rest do with illustrations this file has no system for. The numbers. “Two months free” is 16.7% against the 20% the Change plan segment claims two screens away; nine annual-switch surfaces in the sweep print both prices and the year’s saving as an absolute figure — Motion “$240 → $144, save $480”, Savee “Savings $48”, 1Password both plus Save 20% — and none of them as free months. [⚠] Which exposed that PLAN.billing had three writers and no reader that priced anything. The segment asserted Annual −20% above three rows that kept printing the monthly figure, so pressing it changed which half was dark and nothing else; the invoice list read “Accelerator · annual · $199.00”, three contradictions in one line, twice, a month apart; and the three surfaces described one discount in three sentences. The archive flag’s shape exactly, found the same way. One priceNow(), one sentence, and an annual account gets one invoice row for twelve months. The switch also takes the simulated Stripe round trip every other money control here takes — it had been flipping a variable — and states the charge in full on the way out, which is what Motion does. Still silent on the fee, which is the decision rather than an oversight: close is when the 20% self-sourced or 60/40 house-sourced split comes due [T], that is question 94, and Overview v1.2’s “Why not pay-on-close?” panel may retire the split altogether [~]. [⚠] And the offer’s own button was the fourth surface to hit the page-token-on-a-card trap — Tanya, looking at it: “is this button disabled?” It was not. .btn--outline paints var(--background), a page token, and .mdl paints --card, so every secondary control in every modal was rgb(239,243,248) on white at 1.11:1 with a border at 1.51:1 against its own fill — a filled grey slab wearing a hairline nobody can see. The .alert comment written that same morning had already named this exact case (“the cancel modal’s four reason buttons on .mdl__bd the day before”) and fixed only the alert, so the diagnosis was a day old and the modals had never had it applied. Measured across four of them — screen 8’s four Archive rows and Not now, screen 10’s Cancel request, screen 14’s Switch to annual, screen 16’s See Pro and Wait until reset — eight buttons, all identical. .mdl .btn--outline is transparent now, the border doing its job at 1.68:1, hover untouched, and the same paint came off 28 modal buttons across seven Figma sections so the drawings match the component. A live control that looks dead is worse than an ugly one, because the broker does not press it — and this one is the only place the annual plan is ever offered at the moment it is worth most.
  • The trial start left its own screen, 13 Sep [💡 rec] — the task doc’s screen 2 was drawn as the doc specced it, a dedicated page that replaced the first landing for exactly one navigation: a headline, two sentences and a Post your first deal button. Tanya asked whether that was the right container (modal? toast? home card?) and thirteen trial starts sampled on Mobbin answered it three other ways, none of them a page of its own. The message lands as a dashboard card (Optimal Workshop’s entitlement grid with expiry and Upgrade, Okta’s Welcome to your free trial plan · 23 days left, 1Password’s Let’s get started, HubSpot’s trial guide), a dismissible band above the launcher tiles (Airtable), or a toast beside a persistent rail card (TheyDo) — and the modal is reserved for a trial that cannot start without something: Etsy’s is a billing consent (30 days, then $15/mo on the seller’s bill), Hotjar’s is install the tracking code to start trial, HubSpot’s Sales Hub one carries a real caveat about features taking minutes to appear. Prism’s trial has neither a card nor a setup step, so it had nothing to interrupt for. What the takeover cost was specific: it hid the setup checklist, the network figures (1,500+ lenders, 10,000+ banks, 90,000+ locations) and the whole shape of the app at the one moment curiosity is highest, then discarded its own message forever on the next click — so the entitlement sentence that matters on day six was shown once, on day zero. It is a band at the top of home now. Row 2 is marked Fixed in the doc, and two of its three requirements are carried as written — the sentence and no plan choice. Adapting it to home meant subtracting. The first pass grew what a dashboard card usually grows — four checked entitlement lines, a days-left figure, a draining meter, a See plans door, and a second gold-washed voice for the last three days — and every one of those either added content to a row the doc froze or put a plan door on the one screen that forbids plan choice. All of it came off, and nothing was lost: the countdown is the pill’s job (screen 4), the entitlements belong to the upgrade prompt (screen 6) and Plan & billing (screen 5), the end of the trial to the day-15 modal (screen 13). What is left is one row — info icon, blue chip, the sentence, a dismiss — on the blue info tone, not gold, because it sits directly above the attention card whose gold wash means “look here first” and a notice that asks for nothing should not wear the urgency paint. Two edits on 14 Sep [T]: the reassurance line came off (“When the trial ends you keep every deal on the free plan” — ours rather than the doc’s, and the answer to the question no card needed invites), leaving the band at the doc’s one sentence and leaving the end of the trial stated nowhere before the day-15 modal; and the info tone was raised, because at the old strength it was not reading as blue. The third requirement, One button: Post your first deal, is the one the prototype does not meet (Tanya, 14 Sep). The button lived here for a day and duplicated the Get set up checklist’s own Create your first deal row two cards below it — the same collision that retired the Start-here card on 4 Sep. The first fix had the checklist yield its row to the band; the call reversed it, and the reasoning holds better this way round: the checklist is the surface that knows whether the deal has been made, ticks itself and retires, while a banner button can only ever point. So screen 2 is a notice, not a launcher. Its lifecycle is still the moment, not the calendar: S.trialNew is set at sign-up and cleared the moment a deal is created or the band is dismissed, so it never greets a broker with four deals. Seeded false, since the demo account opens with eleven deals; the sign-up flow raises it. The sentence is the doc’s character for character, em dash included — it ran as a full stop for a few hours under a no-em-dash rule in UI copy, and Tanya retired that rule on 14 Sep, so the Fixed copy stands as written. Two departures go to the walkthrough, not one: the container (the doc says screen 2 is a screen) and the missing button (the doc says one, and it is marked Fixed). Both are ours to justify, and neither is presented as compliance.
  • The cancel flow said the cost after the press, and the page said nothing at all, 16 Sep [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep] — screen 15’s row is “Reason → one retention offer (annual −20% or pause 1 month) → confirm”, marked Fixed, and the hard question in it is whether confirm is a third screen or the confirming click. It was built as a screen for an afternoon and taken out the same day (Tanya: “do we need this screen?”). The case for it: the row’s last word had nothing rendering it, and S.cancelSt was declared null | "reason" | "offer" | "done" with the fourth state drawn by nothing, which reads as the flow recording its own gap. The case against was the evidence gathered for it. Six web cancel flows on Mobbin — Disney+, Open, ElevenLabs, Linktree, Savee, Duolingo — and not one puts a confirm between the offer and the commit; the offer is the friction and every one of them commits on the click that declines it. And NordVPN, whose three-bullet cost panel the step was modelled on, has no offer step at all — the panel is its whole flow, so it replaces the offer rather than following it. Nobody ships both, and taking one reference out of its own shape is how a step gets invented to carry a sentence. What the step was for was real and survives: the cost of leaving existed only in the toast, afterwards, so a broker pressed the button without being told what it costs. It became one line on the offer step — and that line came off too, later the same day; see below. The commit went back to Cancel membership: the label follows the click, so a button that advances must not claim the deed and a button that does the deed must not sound like a step — and with no step after it, naming the act is what ElevenLabs, Linktree and NordVPN all do. [~] S.cancelWhy keeps its writer and has no reader on screen, deliberately: the confirm step quoted it back, and the sentence went with the step, because the broker’s own reason returned to them beside two offers reads as leverage rather than as listening. Its destination is the cancel_started event, which Overview v1.2 names and Chris owes. The outcome was a toast and a gold chip. A fact true for three weeks in a container that expires in seconds — the defect screen 10 closed the same morning — and the chip that survived it read cancels Oct 3 with no statement of what happens then and no way back. Eleven products settle it and none leaves the outcome to a transient: Quicken Resume Subscription beside Expires May 11, Linktree Resubscribe under a band naming the date and the destination tier, Framer turning the current plan’s own button into Reactivate, Perplexity, Duolingo and Savee the same shape. So PLAN.ends split into a date and PLAN.leaving, and the page carries a band: warning for cancel (dated loss, Quicken’s tint), info for pause (nothing is lost, Linktree’s and Netflix’s register), each with the one control the state actually wants. Two things the chip alone had hidden. The fact card said Renews October 3, 2026 four lines under a band saying the account ends that day — three statements about one date, the wrong one in the largest type on the page; the date does not move, only the verb over it, which is what Framer, Perplexity and Quicken all do. And Cancel membership was still offered to a broker who had already cancelled, so the whole flow could be reopened for something that had happened while the page held no control for the thing they would want. Both offers withheld their numbers — “Same plan, two months free” and “Nothing billed, everything kept”: true, and neither answerable by a broker doing arithmetic; worse, two months free was ours, since 20% of a year is 2.4. They print both sides now, from Overview v1.2’s own Billed annually row, which is ElevenLabs’ shape (“from $22/month to just $15.40/month”) and Jasper’s — the same one-month pause, in the same position in the same flow, printing both dates before the press. The pause band carries Netflix’s fact set whole, the most complete of the eleven: when it starts, when it ends, and that billing resumes on its own at the usual price; a pause whose end date the broker cannot see is a cancellation they did not agree to. And S.cancelWhy had no writer — the step whose whole job is to collect one fact discarded it on the click that left; the rows carry it now and the confirm step quotes it back. Then the cost line came off entirely, four versions later and on the same day. Two lines in the body, one line in the body, one line in the footer — it had sat under the pause offer at 12.5px --muted-foreground directly beneath that offer’s 12.5px --muted-foreground sub-line, so proximity did the grouping and got it wrong, and the divider it needed was already drawn in .mdl__ft’s border-top — and then gone [Tanya, 16 Sep: “can we just skip this text?”]. The doc settles it. Screen 15’s row is reason → one offer → confirm, marked Fixed, and it does not ask for a disclaimer; the deals-go-read-only sentence is screen 13’s row, which is where it is marked Fixed and where it is built. The line was ours, and the references are split rather than behind it — Linktree and NordVPN state the cost before the commit, the other four do not. What made it safe to drop is the after-state: the band states the same fact the moment the modal closes, with Keep Accelerator beside it, so the press reverses in one click; the rule about naming a cost before a button offers it is about a gate the broker cannot undo, and this is not one. [~] What it costs is that the read-only count — the one consequence a broker cannot guess — is not in front of them at the press; worth raising if the flow is ever tested. The detour left nothing behind, which was the point: .mdl__ft--stack and nd/ro came out with it rather than staying as rules and counts with no call site, and the Note property added to Modal/Sectioned for that one sentence came out too [Tanya, 16 Sep] — a library component carrying an option nothing uses is the same defect one level up, and visible to everyone rather than to this file.Drawn in Figma as a four-frame Monetization section — the two dialog steps and the two after-states — and the Account page’s own two cancel frames synced to match, after the first pass edited only the clones and let the originals go stale within the hour. [~] The library’s only gold Badge is section-gold, an uppercase section pill, so the leaving chip is an outline instance with paint overrides and the gap is a question — the same one the trial-expiry section recorded for its muted chip.
  • The trial expiry got its read-only half, 16 Sep [💡 rec · Mobbin 16 Sep] — screen 13’s row is four columns wide: a modal, on any page, day 15, carrying one sentence marked Fixed — “You’re on Essential. Your 4 deals are saved; 3 are read-only until you upgrade.” Three of the four were wrong here. The Fixed copy was paraphrased, rewritten into three sentences with the slot rule folded in and a never-gate list appended; it is carried character for character now with its two counts substituted, the same treatment screen 2’s sentence gets and for the same reason. The trigger did not exist: data-expprev survived the 15 Sep removal of the walkthrough strips and lost the button that set it, so the only thing that could open screen 13 was a handler nothing could fire — this strip has been claiming since then that day-15 expiry was previewable on Plan & billing, and it was not. The trigger is state now (trialOver(), a trial with no days left, on whatever page the broker is standing) plus one real product control: choosing Essential from the trial lands a broker in exactly the state the row describes, so it gets the row’s screen rather than dropping them into it silently. And nothing was read-only. data-expok set the tier and closed the dialog; every control on every deal stayed live. The same write-only shape archive had that morning — a sentence with no reader — except this sentence is the doc’s, so the prototype was making the Fixed copy false. A deal over the cap now wears a muted Read-only chip on the row and the card beside the Archived one; its page opens with an .alert--warning naming the deal that holds the slot; its status is a fact in a muted pill rather than a select; Edit deal, Send loan request and the execution-support row answer with the gate; and every other write path into it — status from the deals table, saving or unsaving a lender, an outreach value — is caught by one backstop in the click handler rather than by threading a flag through four shared surfaces that also serve the deal-less case, which is how a flag ends up half-applied. Which deal keeps the slot is ambiguity 3, broker’s pick or most recent, unspecced either way. Newest is the default and the broker can change it — from the banner on any read-only deal, undoably. It was first built as a picker inside the modal and came out the same day (Tanya asked where the pattern came from; the honest answer was that the row shape came from _Body/8, the words were inherited from the 13 Sep body, and the button was new and nothing asked for it). The row is marked Fixed, and this strip records the opposite call on screen 2 four days earlier — “adapting it meant subtracting… every one of those either added content to a row the doc froze”. Growing a one-sentence frozen row into a 356px dialog with a control was that rule applied backwards. The modal is 265px now: the Fixed sentence, one line naming which deal holds the slot and where that can be changed, two buttons. The fact stays, the control moves — the alternative is silence, and silence is the failure this feature exists to avoid: Miro makes “any additional boards view-only and locked for editing”, silently, on the three most recently created, so the rule picks which of your work dies. Trello reopens what you closed, Figma restores from Drafts, Productboard hands the choice back — the reversible majority all let you say which work survives. Six OCR sweeps on Mobbin settled three more things. The footer pair is Productboard’s, read off the screen: its expired state offers [Switch to free plan] outline and [Choose a plan] filled, which is this modal’s pair with our plan names on it — and it carries a third escape we do not have and did not invent, “Need more time? Extend your trial.” No close ×, because a wall is not dismissible, the clearest rule out of the metered-surface sweep and true twice over here since the plan has already changed underneath the broker; Continue on Essential is the dismiss and it names what dismissing means. And the vocabulary is unsourced [~]: read-only returns zero screens and upgrade to edit zero, while view only returns twenty-four and every one of them is a sharing permission — Dropbox Dash, MagicPath, Gemini Notebook — not a plan state. Nobody ships these words for this meaning. We are keeping read-only because the doc marks the sentence Fixed, but it is a term the market has already given to something else and that is a question for Tony, not a detail. Still open, stated not invented [~]: ambiguity 8 — firing on any page means that on day 15 this is the first thing after login, against the doc’s own rule that nothing gates at login; it reads as a deliberate exception and the doc never says so, and an exception nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from an oversight. The banner was a warning, and warned nine times [💡 rec] — it shipped alert--warning, which is the wrong register twice: read-only is a condition of the object rather than a warning, and the band is up on nine deals out of ten permanently, so every deal but one opened amber while the muted chip on the row was stating the same fact quietly. This file had already made that argument the other way for the deal cap — “a cap of one has no approach… a banner on the second state would be permanently on”. It is .alert--state now, the base alert, and the tint is gone from the lock too: it kept an amber glyph for one turn on the argument that an icon-only tint is the end of the component’s own tint the border and the icon, leave the prose alone line rather than a departure from it — a sound component argument and the wrong product one, because this file already ships a lock strip. .oppnote--gate, the contact gate on the banker drawer (Tanya, 14 Sep: “use this ui with one line text”), draws its lock in --muted-foreground, and two locks in one product both meaning gated, one slate and one amber, is an inconsistency no reader can resolve. The lock carries meaning by being a lock. What did not move is the ground: the gate’s muted fill computes to rgb(238,240,245) and .btn--outline paints var(--background), rgb(239,243,248) — one and three and three apart, so the outline button would render as a border around nothing, the same token trap as the four outline buttons that read as filled slabs on a white modal ground with the ground moved the other way. The gate can recede that far because it has no action and captions the masked Email and Phone rows directly above it; this band is the only statement of the fact on its page and holds the two controls that end it. What that measurement then caught on the ground that did stay [💡 rec]: .btn--outline paints a page token and .alert paints --card, so Make this the active deal was rgb(239,243,248) inside rgb(255,255,255) — 1.11:1, a filled grey slab rather than an outline button. Third surface to hit it: the cancel modal’s four reason rows on .mdl__bd, the plan card’s pill on the rail, and now the band. The plan card’s comment already wrote the rule — “the outline variant is built for a page, and there is no page behind it here”. .alert .btn--outline is transparent now, the border doing the work it was drawn for at 1.68:1, hover untouched. The page’s three other action alerts carry a single filled button and never had the problem. And its CTA said the opposite of what it does: Make this active reads as adding a deal, and active is the cap’s own unit (10 active · 1 allowed), when what the control does is move the slot off another deal and take that deal’s editing away. It reads Make this the active deal, the description names the cost before the button offers it, and the slot carries the documented pair — [Upgrade to Pro] [Delete a project] in the guidance, [Upgrade] [Archive] on this file’s own second-deal gate — where it had only the free escape, which had made it the one gate in the seventeen with no control for the paid path. The page’s other alert-with-action, the fair-use cap at 100%, uses a filled button too, so the grey outline had been the minority position on its own page as well. Full sweep: trial-expiry-pattern-research.
  • One inline banner, not two, 14 Sep [💡 rec] — Tanya asked whether the design system has an info banner. It does not, and the asking caught a duplicate: the trial band had been hand-built a day earlier beside .pbanner, the profile page’s “claim your listing” strip, with the same shell — a lead slot, a dismissible body, no required action. They are one component now. .pbanner took a __tx body so it can hold either a single sentence with an inline link or a title plus a muted line, its lead slot accepts an icon or a Badge, and the trial band took the system’s info blue rather than the neutral it wore for a day — that neutral had been invented to avoid colliding with the attention card’s gold, when there was already a colour for “here is a fact.” What the check actually found is a system-level hole. components/ui/alert.tsx ships two variants, destructive and a default that is bg-card text-card-foreground — an untinted card, not an info tone — and it is imported once in the whole frontend, in pro-license-dialog.tsx, as destructive. The Figma library carries no Alert, banner, notice or callout component at all [verified 14 Sep against a control query, since a library search that finds nothing proves nothing on its own]. Meanwhile these screens already need four tones — info (.pbanner), warning (.lbanner), success (.lbanner--live, .okpanel) and attention (.card--att) — and hand-roll every one, because globals.css has --color-warning and --color-success as bare foreground colours with no paired surface or border, and no info token whatsoever. That is the same inline-hex defect already raised for Badge’s section variants. Merging our two is a prototype-local fix to a system-level gap and will diverge from whatever ships; question 95 puts both halves to Chris — whether alert.tsx gains info / success / warning variants, and whether the four tones get surface + border + foreground triples as tokens so a variant set can be written without hex.
  • The Alert component, 14 Sep [💡 rec] — question 95’s own option A, built rather than described, so Chris can look at it. Anatomy is shadcn’s alert.tsx, the component the repo already has: a two-column grid whose first column is zero-wide so an alert with no icon has no leading gutter and widens to 16px when one is present (grid-cols-[0_1fr] + has-[>svg]:, drawn here with :has()), gap-x 12 / gap-y 2, rounded-lg, px-4 py-3, title and description both col-start-2, title font-medium with tight tracking, description muted, icon nudged translate-y-0.5. Variants are ReUI’s — @reui is already registered in the frontend’s components.json, so upstream this is an install, not a build — each tone formed the same way: border at ~30% of the tone, background at ~5%, icon at full tone, prose left as foreground, which is why four tones can sit on one page without shouting. Tokens are Prism’s, the half ReUI cannot supply: its own cssVars ship violet for info, emerald for success and yellow for warning. Bound instead to --color-success and --color-warning as globals.css ships them, --destructive, and a new --color-info — brand-navy-800, 10.4:1 on white. Navy-600 was tried first and washed to grey at tint strength; the info mix also had to go from ReUI’s 4% to 9%, and then to 15% on 14 Sep [T], because that formula assumes a vivid hue and Prism’s blue is a dark navy: at /9 the fill computed to rgb(232,238,244), twelve points of blue over red — blue by measurement, grey to the eye. The border went to /38 with it, or the edge would have vanished into a fill that strong. Worth saying rather than glossing: navy-800 is the same hex as --color-congress-blue, which the landing playbook spends on the borrower audience accent — the two never meet on a drawn screen, but it is the token to move if Chris wants them apart. Two additions are ours, both named in the question: a dismiss column (neither shadcn nor ReUI has one, and both our banners need it) and a Badge slot, which began in the icon column as a substitute for a glyph and moved inline to the head of the title on 14 Sep [T], once the trial notice wanted both an icon and a chip and one column could not hold them. The icon slot is the tone’s own signal and reads down a page of stacked alerts; a badge labels the sentence it sits on, so the badge is the one that moves. Baseline-aligned there, which is what puts its text on the title’s own baseline — and the badge’s 23.4px line box against the title’s 18.9px is why the icon needs 4px of nudge rather than shadcn’s 2px, scoped to .alert:has(.alert__badge) so an alert whose title wraps keeps the original; ReUI’s AlertAction is carried as .alert__act. It replaced three hand-rolled strips — .pbanner (profile listing, trial start) and .okpanel (deal created) — and took over the create form’s Your deal could be stronger warning. What deliberately did not move: .warnpanel, because four of its five uses are prototype commentary about what is undrawn or unanswered, which is not a notice the product shows a broker; and .lbanner, whose --stack variant carries a review tracker rather than a sentence. .card--att is a card of rows, not an alert, and stays.
  • The facet counts came off the rail, 14 Sep [💡 rec] — Tanya, pointing at the number column down the rail’s right edge. Every option row had printed its own live count, and the rail is five facets deep, so a broker scanning for a value read a column of arithmetic first: with six options open per facet that is up to thirty numbers on a control whose whole content is thirty-odd words. The numbers were also the least stable thing on the page — they move on every tick of every other facet by design, so the column flickered while the labels beside it sat still. The count itself is not removed, only its printing: lCountFor still runs, and it still does the two jobs that made the rail worth building over the bar — it orders the six options that lead, so what the network actually holds sits at the top of State rather than Alabama, and — until later the same day — it dimmed a value your other filters had emptied. The dim went too, four notes below; ordering is what is left. Those were always the load-bearing half of the argument; the digit was the audit trail for it. What is genuinely lost is the magnitude: the rail now says Texas is reachable and Idaho is not, and no longer says 21 against 3 — so a broker cannot tell a deep market from a thin one without running the filter. [~] Worth one line at the walkthrough, because the counted-checkbox sketch that started this rail was Tanya’s own (13 Sep) and this reverses half of it; if the magnitude turns out to matter, the cheaper restoration is the count on hover or on the facet header, not back on every row. The applied-count badge on a folded facet header is untouched — it counts your selections, not the network, and it is the one thing keeping a shut facet honest.
  • The applied chips moved out of the rail, 14 Sep [💡 rec · comp 14 Sep] — Tanya, looking at seven chips wrapped over four rows at the top of the rail: “do other products also use this logic for selected filters?” Twenty-four faceted surfaces read on Mobbin that day. Fourteen echo the selection as removable chips, so the pattern is well precedented; the placement was the minority. Eleven of the fourteen put the echo in the results column — Klarna, Care.com, Etsy, Urban Outfitters, Uxcel, Pinterest, Employment Hero, Gorgias, Aboard, Copy.ai, Base44. Workable is our arrangement almost exactly (rail heading, an Applied filters block with Clear all, then the collapsible facets under it) and Walmart does the same inside its All-filters drawer. Apollo is the third answer and the most interesting: it distributes the echo, parking each chip inside its own facet section beneath a per-facet applied badge. Two more — Google Drive and Turo — carry the value in the control itself and need no echo at all; Behance, Dribbble, Amplitude, Jira and Unity draw a rail and echo nothing. The deciding argument is width, not the tally. Seven chips wrap to four rows in a 258px rail and fit on one or two in a ~1050px column, so the identical information costs the page a quarter of the height — and it was pushing State below the fold in a rail that had just been quietened by taking the option counts off, immediately above this note. The second argument is what the chips are for: in the results column they answer why is this list what it is beside the list and, on a deal, beside the 3 bankers · 3 accounts count they explain (the network page’s own count came off within the day — the note below); in the rail they answered it beside the ticked checkboxes that already say it, making three representations of one state — header badge, chips, checkbox. They sit below the toolbar’s own border so they group with the rows rather than with the controls, and they render in the empty state too, where dropping one chip is a cheaper correction than the Clear all that state offers. The chips gained their facet name, Workable’s and Uxcel’s own anatomy: bare values could not say which facet they came from — Office-Owner/User reads like a job title rather than a property type — and four states in a row now read as one dimension narrowed four ways rather than four unrelated proper nouns. The label is muted and the value is not, so the repetition recedes. Ordering needed nothing: the builder already walked LFILTERS in Tony’s 26 Aug facet order, so the row reads in the same sequence as the rail beneath it. Clear all stayed in the rail header — Care.com and Workable both keep the clear inside the filter surface, and a second one riding the chip row would be two controls for one state a screen-width apart. [~] What this gives up, and it is the reason the block was in the rail: a value inside a folded facet (Execution type and Source are shut by default) is no longer legible from the rail alone. The applied-count badge on the folded header still declares that something is set, and the chip above the table still names it — but the two are now at opposite ends of the screen. Apollo’s per-facet arrangement is the fix if that turns out to bite.
  • The rail was audited against the design system, 14 Sep [💡 rec · repo Sep 14] — Tanya, pointing at a crop of the State facet: “are those counters and checkboxes from the current Prism library?” None of the three were. The checkboxes were bare <input type="checkbox"> at 14px with accent-color, which paints the operating system’s own box — square corners, its own tick, no border or shadow unchecked — where ui/checkbox.tsx is Radix at size-4 with rounded-[4px], border-input, shadow-xs and a lucide CheckIcon size-3.5. The file already owned a faithful copy, .chk / .bx, and was using it on Group by account forty pixels away on the same screen. This is the same defect the Details-tab editor was corrected for on 31 Aug, reintroduced on a new surface, which says the problem is adoption rather than a slip: nothing in the file makes the component the easier thing to reach for. The two pills — the applied count on a facet header and the Filters N badge in the rail header — were hand-rolled copies of Badge at two different sizes, 11px/700 and 11.5px/600, against badge.tsx’s rounded-full px-2 py-0.5 text-xs font-medium. Both are the .badge component now and set nothing of their own, and then neither was a pill at all (Tanya, same hour: “do we have some alternative to those counters?”, then “explore how other products use this”). The first answer demoted the per-facet badges to --outline and kept the rail total filled, on the argument that the split read as a hierarchy. Twenty-four faceted products on Mobbin settled it differently [comp 14 Sep]: nobody paints a filter count as a filled pill. Apollo writes Hide Filters 3 and, per facet, a bare × 1; Plain writes Filters 4; Care.com Filters (7); Selfridges Brand 4; Xero, Etsy and Lyssna right-align a bare numeral; Linear uses no number at all, just the sentence 16 issues hidden by filters. The heaviest treatment in the whole sample is Clay’s pale tint, and Juicebox reduces it to a dot. So both counts are now label plus muted numeral, which is the convention and also the honest weight — a count is an annotation on a heading, not a thing to act on. The facet count gained a word: State · 3 selected, Clay’s own wording minus its pill. A lone 3 eight lines above Show all 51 does not say what it counts — and removing the per-option counts that morning made it more ambiguous, not less: while every row carried its own number, State 3 was obviously a different kind of number from Texas 21; alone in the facet it has nothing to contrast against. The rail header needs no word, since Filters 4 can only mean four filters. [~] Held as a separate question: Apollo pairs its per-facet count with a clear-this-facet ×, which the rail has no equivalent of — today one facet can only be cleared chip by chip above the table, or by Clear all, which takes out everything. That is a new control rather than a paint change and was not smuggled in with one. Filled navy is the heaviest paint in the file — it is what a primary button wears — and it had been sitting on up to five headers in the quietest column on the page, reporting a fact the ticks below it and the chips above the table both already carry. Three lighter treatments were drawn and not taken: showing the count only on a folded facet (the accordion-summary convention, and the one place the number cannot be got otherwise), naming the values rather than counting them (Apollo and Uxcel do this, but a 258px header truncates past one and a half values), and dropping it outright (which leaves a folded facet filtering with nothing in the rail saying so). Demotion keeps every state legible and costs nothing. The real find was underneath. .chk named two components: the Checkbox at line 451 and the home setup-checklist row eight hundred lines later, and since the checklist rule loads last it was silently winning — every .chk in the file, nine of them, had been inheriting the row’s display:flex, its 9px/10px padding, its −10px margins and its hover wash instead of the component’s inline-grid. Nothing looked broken because .bx carries the visible box, so it paid out as checkboxes with a clickable-row hover state and inexplicable negative margins. The checklist row is .setuprow now; the Checkbox keeps the short name, because it is the primitive and the other is one card’s row. Left alone, and it is a decision [💡 rec]: the facet search boxes stay at 30px rather than becoming .inp at h-9/36px. shadcn ships no small Input, and a 36px field stacked above 12.5px option rows in a 258px rail would out-weigh the values it filters — a genuine density problem rather than drift, and the honest fix is a sm Input variant in input.tsx, not a local override pretending to be one. [~] Figma cannot be matched either way: Prism — Design System has no Checkbox at all — twenty hits, every one from someone else’s kit — confirmed against a control query, since a library search that finds nothing proves nothing on its own. The code side is fine, so this is an unbuilt page in 02 · Primitives rather than a question for Chris; it is recorded in [[design-system-setup]] beside the Alert gap that is one.
  • The row count came off the network toolbar, 14 Sep (Tanya) — 27 bankers · 20 accounts, right-aligned in the results bar on /lenders, and its 0 of 27 bankers twin in the empty state. Third thing removed from this page in a day, and the same argument each time: the surface was stating one fact in several places at once. The network size is already on screen — the Network 27 tab chip carries it, permanently and in the place a broker looks to switch source — and what narrowed the list is now spelt out value by value in the applied chips directly beneath, which arrived an hour earlier. The count sat between them restating both. Matches and Saved keep theirs, and the distinction is not squeamishness about repetition: on a deal the two units are the account rollup’s own ambiguity — one number silently meaning people on one screen and institutions on the next is exactly what the rollup introduced, and the pair is there to answer it. On the network page the tab chip has already counted the bankers and the accounts are a grouping the broker just switched on. [~] What it costs: a filtered result has no printed size any more. Narrow to four rows and the page shows four rows — there is no table footer here and no pagination, so a broker who wants the tally counts it. That is cheap at this scale and would not be at three hundred; if paging ever lands, the count comes back with it, and the honest home for it then is the table footer beside the pager rather than the toolbar. Settings inherits the margin-left:auto the count was carrying, so the right edge of the bar is unchanged.
  • The rail narrowed to 224, 14 Sep (Tanya: “make filters panel narrower if possible”) — it was 258. What sets the width is the option labels, so that is what was measured rather than guessed: 224 leaves 200px for a label after the 16px checkbox and its 8px gap, and none of the seventeen values a rail shows by default comes within 30px of that — the longest, Retail-Multi Tenant, needs 112. Expanded, with all five facets open and every Show all taken, 96 of the 99 values in the vocabulary still sit on one line; three wrap, and one of those three — Manufactured Housing / Mobile Home Park, 254px — wrapped at 258 as well. So the change costs two wrapped rows in a state a broker reaches by asking for the full list. Truncation is not a risk at any width near this: the longest unbreakable word in the whole vocabulary is Office-Owner/User at 113px. The facet headers were the other candidate constraint and clear it comfortably — the worst case, Property type · 3 selected, is 157px against 204 of header space. The 34px goes to the table, which is the half of this screen that is actually short: the same measurement that produced the auto-collapsing nav had the card 111px short at 1440 (854 against a table that will not compress below 965), and 34 of that is now back — recovered from the column that had slack rather than from the nav. [~] Nothing else moves — the 16px gap, the shut-rail rule and the one-column breakpoint are all unchanged, and the rail is the only thing on the page measured in a fixed track.
  • The facet group captions came off, 14 Sep (Tanya: “remove these subheaders”) — expanding Property type printed RETAIL, MULTIFAMILY & RESIDENTIAL and six more over its values. Three arguments, and the first is the one that shows in a screenshot: uppercase and letter-spaced, they were the loudest type in the rail, sitting above a column of 12.5px sentence-case values whose whole job is to be scanned — the same weight problem as the option counts and the filled badges removed earlier the same day, and the third time this column has been quietened. Second, they rode one facet of five, so Property type read as a different kind of list from State directly above it. Third, the grouping carries little here: four of the eight groups hold one or two values, so a caption often bought a heading per pair — Retail over Retail-Multi Tenant and Retail-Single Tenant, which the values already say. Nothing about the order changed, which is what made this a safe cut: PROPERTY_TYPES is PROPERTY_GROUPS flattened, verified value for value, so the grouped branch was only ever laying captions over the sequence the flat branch prints anyway. The grouping is not lost — f.groups still feeds the MultiSelect accordion on the deal form, and that is the version worth keeping: there a group is a control with a tri-state checkbox and a child count that ticks all six residential types at once [💡 rec · comp 28 Aug · Janover], where in the rail it was a caption that did nothing. [~] If grouping is ever wanted back on this surface, that is the form it should take.
  • Both design-system defects turned up once more in the rail, 14 Sep (Tanya, two screenshots) — and neither was a new mistake, which is the point worth recording. “Use proper close icon”: the facet search fields are type="search", so Chrome draws ::-webkit-search-cancel-button on its own — a heavy X painted in the input’s own navy at a size nobody chose. This is the exact defect fixed on 8 Sep, when four copies of the page-level search box were folded into srchBox() and the native clear was suppressed and replaced with XSM in an .ms__x. The facet field is a fifth search input that never went through that function, so it kept the browser’s control. It now suppresses the native button and draws the same one, at right: 6px with 26px of right padding to sit in, and clearing returns focus to the field — the query was wrong, not finished. It needed its own click branch (data-lfqclr) because a facet query lives in the S.lFq map rather than at a top-level state key, which is what srchBox’s id-doubles-as-state-key convention depends on. “Change count style to outlined”: the applied count on the new Hide filters button was a hand-rolled navy pill at 11px/700 — a fourth copy of Badge, built the same hour the other two were being replaced by the component. It is .badge badge--outline now, and the only local property left is tabular figures so the button does not twitch between 1 and 4. [~] What both say is what the 31 Aug checkbox repeat said and the audit note above restated: the defect recurs because nothing in the file makes the component the easier thing to reach for. A new control gets built, its author writes the pill inline, and it is caught only when someone looks at a screenshot. The cheap guard is a grep before shipping any new control — border-radius: 9999px outside the .badge block, and type="search" outside srchBox.
  • A ticked option stopped dimming, 14 Sep (Tanya: “why do some checkboxes become disabled?”) — they were not disabled, and that was the whole defect. .lopt.zero drops a row to 62% opacity when lCountFor returns 0, which reads no lender has this value, given your other filters — the one job the counts kept when they stopped printing. Nothing excluded a checked row from it, and a checked row can go to zero the moment two facets conflict: tick Nevada and North Carolina, then tick a property type nobody in either state lends on, and both states fall to zero while still ticked. What that paints is precisely Radix’s disabled control — muted label, muted box — so the two rows the broker most needs to click, the ones to untick to get results back, were the two that looked unclickable. The empty result list beneath them was the corroborating evidence: it says nothing matched, which makes unavailable the natural reading of the dim. The first fix exempted ticked values: a value in the set never took .zero. It lasted ten minutes (Tanya, looking at an expanded State list: “still dimmed”), and the correction is worth keeping because it is a lesson about scope. Exempting the ticked row fixed the worst reading and left the cause standing — 62% opacity on a label and its box is what a disabled control looks like, and an unticked dimmed row asks exactly the same wrong question as a ticked one. A rail option is never disabled: every one of the 51 is clickable, and clicking a zero is a legitimate move that lands on an empty list which names its own cause. So the dim is gone outright, and .lopt.zero with it. [~] The count still does two things, neither of them a paint: zeros sort below live values, so the six a facet shows by default exclude them almost always, and a zero is only ever on screen once Show all is taken or a search is typed. What is genuinely lost is the warning one step earlier — scanning the full 51, a broker can no longer see which states are empty before clicking one. That is the same magnitude loss the note above records for the printed counts, now complete: lCountFor orders the list and nothing else. If it wants restoring, the honest form is the number back on the row, not a paint that claims the control is dead.
  • A long option list bounds itself, 14 Sep [💡 rec · comp 14 Sep] (Tanya: “this list looks too long”) — Show all 51 was appending fifty-one rows to the page. Measured before touching it: the State facet alone reached 1389px and took the rail from 866 to 1991 in a 901px viewport, so a broker who opened the full list had pushed Property type, Loan amount, Execution type and Source out of reach and had to collapse State again to get back to them. All five expanded came to 3095px, three and a half screens of rail. Twenty-four faceted surfaces read on Mobbin, and not one lets a long vocabulary grow the page. They split two ways: bound it and scroll inside — Klook’s country dialog, X’s Countries panel, WhatsApp’s Region sheet, Revolut’s citizenship list (Suggested above All), Deel’s filter modal, Square’s drawer, AWS’s continent-grouped menu, Zoho’s scrolling rail — or replace the list with a type-ahead, which is Airbnb, Turo, Threads, Airtasker and Posh. A third group reveals in place (Show 6 more, Show 20 more at Coursera; Show more at Tripadvisor; See more at Midjourney) but only where the vocabulary is tens. Our anatomy was already Klarna’s — facet search, six leading values, Show all 37 — and only the behaviour of Show all differed: theirs opens a bounded surface, ours grew the column. Now: past ten rows the list bounds itself and scrolls inside. Re-measured on the shipped fraction: State expanded takes the rail to 976 rather than 1991, and all five open and expanded to 1418 rather than 3095, the three caps summing to 780. [~] The 966/1495 pair this note first carried was taken under the flat 250 cap; 250 × 3 is only 30 less than today’s caps, so 1495 cannot be reconciled with 1418 by the cap alone and something else about that reading differed. 1418 is the measured number. Three of the five facets ever hit the cap (State 51, Property type 24, Execution type 17); Loan amount and Source are too short to reach it. Two details are load-bearing. The cap is on the list, not the facet body, so the search field and Show fewer sit outside the scroll — the two controls that get a broker out of a long list are the two a scroll must never carry off. And the scroll position survives a tick: render() rebuilds the list from scratch, so without carrying scrollTop across, ticking Wyoming threw you back to Alabama — the same problem the facet search already solves for its caret. The cut was wrong at first and took a second pass (Tanya, same day: “show 50% of last item so users understand that section is scrollable”). 250 is exactly ten 25px rows, so the box ended between rows and the edge read as the end of the list — and on macOS the overlay scrollbar stays invisible until you touch the trackpad, so nothing else was advertising the scroll. The fix is a part row, and it could not be arithmetic alone: a budget of 25px × 10.5 lands on an exact half in State, but Property type has one value that wraps to two lines and the same number cut 4px into a row there — a hairline, which is the flat edge again. So the stylesheet states the budget and cutFacetLists() snaps to it after render, ending the box at the same fraction of whichever row the budget falls inside, whatever that row’s height. The fraction settled at 40%, walked down from a half to a quarter and back up (Tanya, same day: “show 50%”, “show 25%, not 50”, “change to 30%”, “change to 40%”) — now one constant, LFCUT = 0.4, with 25px × 10.4 as the matching CSS budget, giving State 260, Property type 269, Execution type 251, each measured at 0.37–0.42 of its cut row. [~] What the fractions actually buy, since 4px of every row is .lopt’s top padding before anything draws: at 0.25 only ~2px of checkbox survives and it reads as a hairline; at 0.3, ~3.5px, a box but no text; at 0.4, 10px — the checkbox clears its corner radius and the caps-height of the label shows, so the row reads as clipped rather than as a rendering artefact. That is the threshold worth remembering: the cue stops being a sliver once the text starts. LFCUT is the one number to move, with the CSS budget kept in step. The quarter pass exposed a real bug, worth keeping: the snap read its budget from clientHeight, which is an integer property, so a 257.5px cap came back as 258 — exactly a row boundary in Property type. No row straddled it, the snap silently did nothing, and that one facet fell back to the flat cut the whole mechanism exists to avoid, while State and Execution type looked fine because their budgets happened to round mid-row. It now reads getComputedStyle().maxHeight. Reading a fractional CSS length back through an integer DOM property is a half-pixel lie — clientHeight and offsetHeight round, getBoundingClientRect() and getComputedStyle() do not. The lesson is the one the dimming pass taught: a rule derived from the one case in front of you is not a rule — uniform rows were an assumption about State, and the facet next to it broke them. [~] Held as a separate question: dropping Show all for State entirely and leaning on the search box, which is what Airbnb and Turo do. Fifty-one states are browsable and brokers think in states, so the list earns its place for now.
  • Three actions, one card header — the deal’s services moved out, 14 Sep [💡 rec] — Tanya asked where the three buttons in the Lenders on this deal header came from, and the answer was three different places: Request execution support is a shipped control [T · 5 Aug] (OpsRequestButtons.tsx), Request branded memo is the task doc’s screen 10 [task doc] with its label taken verbatim, and Send loan request is ours [~] — the doc gives the cap, nothing in the product sends a package to N lenders. Three origins had become one row, and only one of them acts on that card. The card keeps the action whose object it holds: Send loan request, the page’s single filled button, over the saved list it sends to. The other two are deal-level — a memo about the deal, a team that works the whole deal — and the doc files both under Deal details, not under the lenders panel; they move to an overflow menu in the page header, the file’s own .rowkebab / .cardmenu anatomy, unchanged from the deal rows and the three lender tables. The arrangement is the market’s [comp 14 Sep · Mobbin]: Zoho CRM’s record header runs one filled button, two outline, then an overflow; Pipedrive and Apollo both park the once-per-record actions behind …. Edit deal gave up its fill in the same pass, since two filled buttons a section apart were arguing about what the deal was for. The row actions followed, 14 Sep (Tanya, pointing at a column of navy Save to deal buttons) — a filled button repeated down every row is a column of primaries, and a page claiming twelve primaries has none. The save verb is outline now in all five lists it repeats down: the matches table, the lender network table (Tanya again, minutes later — the same column of navy, and that page has no deal to act on at all, so it is a list to read rather than a call to make), the account page’s contact rows, and both directory lists, the deal-scoped Prospector door and the Prospector tab. The fill is spent once per surface, and three keep it on purpose: the select bar’s Save to deal, which exists only while a selection does and is the point of having made one, and the quick-view drawer and account page, where the band under the name is one action on one record rather than the same action on twenty. The contact profile’s save was already outline for a different reason — it lives inside the history card, so it is a card’s action, not the page’s. Tanya pushed back — is the save not that page’s main action? It is, and the answer is that main and filled are different claims: six results lists whose whole purpose is a per-row save were sampled [comp 14 Sep · Mobbin] — Wellfound, Evernote, Faire, komoot, KAYAK, Juicebox — and not one fills the row control; KAYAK spends its fill on a different action entirely. Repetition is the emphasis: twenty-seven buttons in an aligned column cannot be missed, so the fill would buy weight and no discovery. The network table has no row selection, so unlike the matches table it cannot state its own verb at page scope; giving it the select bar would put the fill back exactly where it earns its keep — 12 selected · Save to a deal — and is the better answer to that question than repainting the rows. [~] Outline rather than the secondary variant, because outline is already this file’s second weight — Find lenders, View profile, Hide from this deal all wear it, and a grey fill would open a third. State does not live in the menu: a requested service prints as a badge under the deal name — Memo on its way · 2 business days, Ops working on it — because a shut menu cannot tell a broker something is already under way; the row stays listed inside, disabled, carrying its own state for whoever comes back to order it twice. That is the shipped rule showing through, one open request per deal on a partial-unique index. The non-Pro memo row stays visible with a quiet Pro at its right rather than disappearing — the doc’s own principle is that a gate is discoverable where the action is. And every control label is sentence case from here (Tanya, standing rule): Request execution support, Find lenders, Edit deal, Delete deal, Change status all lost their Title Case, including Find Lenders, which is the shipped product’s own string — the word choice is Tony’s and survives, the casing is ours and does not. Tier names (Pro, Essential) and the Prospector stay capitalised: they are names, not labels. Open [~]: the doc specs screen 9’s label as Send to 3 · Upgrade to send to 12 and marks it Fixed; the count and the upsell live in the modal footer here instead, where the broker has actually picked recipients — a deliberate deviation Olesia should see rather than inherit.
  • The deal checklist stopped under-promising, 14 Sep [T] — Tony, pinned on the Create your first deal row: “add ‘location’”. The sub-line read A name, an amount and a property type are enough to start, and the form it launches blocks on five fields, not three: name && amt > 0 && property && state && zip. Zip being required is his own call [T · 31 Aug], so a broker who supplied exactly what the checklist named would have hit a validation error on the first deal of their first session. This was a factual error in our copy rather than a wording preference, which is why it goes in without argument. One noun for two fields: a location covers state and zip, because location is three fields at two strengths in that form — state and zip both gate the save, city is a soft gap that offers Save anyway — and a first-session line should name the broker’s object, not the schema’s. [💡 rec] The deeper fix is not taken here: the sentence is hand-written while the profile row two lines above derives its counter from profGaps(), so this list will drift again the next time the validation moves. Deriving it from the same hard predicate the save checks is the durable answer and is a change to the form, not to the copy. [~] The matcher preview’s own line is left alone and is not the same claim — draftReady() needs state and not zip, because matching is state-scoped, so Add loan amount, property type and state is exactly true where it sits.
  • The listing came out of the setup count, 14 Sep [T] — Tony, pinned on the Complete your profile row, 9 Sep: “Change this sentence ‘2 to add….’ to read ‘complete your public profile (only for Pro members)’”. The gate is his and it is right; the sentence could not sit where he put it, and the reason is that he was reading one render of a ten-branch expression. That sub-line is profGaps() counting ten fields across three sections, and the sandbox account happened to be down to its last two, which are the listing pair. On a new account the same line reads 8 to add: your name, your company… — name, company, phone, state, property types, executions, loan range, states covered, none of them Pro-only. They prefill every deal and drive lender matching on every tier. Adopting his sentence would have told an Essential broker to skip eight fields we need filled, and pinned the row at a permanent 1 of 2, since two of its ten checks sit behind a gate that tier cannot pass. An uncompletable row on a completion checklist is a defect whatever sentence is under it. The fix is subtraction, not addition: profGaps() is split at the point of use and only coreGaps, the eight every tier can fill, drives the row and the N of 2. The gate is not restated on home at all — it is on the listing section, in his own words, where he pinned it the same day. A fourth row was built here first, and removed within the hour [💡 rec · withdrawn] — Get listed for borrowers, below the denominator, a task on Pro and a Pro-pilled upgrade door on every other tier. Tanya asked the question that killed it: when did he ask for this? He did not. Both of his 9 Sep comments ask for a sentence; neither asks for a row, and the label, the copy, the pill and the upsell placement were all ours. It had been reasoned into place off the back of his comment and presented as though it followed from it, which is the failure mode the provenance tags exist to prevent — a [💡 rec] wearing a [T]. It also contradicted its own argument in one detail: the non-Pro variant still drew an empty completion circle a broker on that tier could never fill. Recorded rather than deleted because the row may be worth proposing to him as a proposal — the first screen a new broker sees is the cheapest upsell placement in the product, and that case should be made to Tony, not smuggled in under a copy fix. [~] Still open on a second surface: the profile nav badge beside Public listing reads 2 to add on every tier, because it counts gaps per section with no tier test. Same defect, and it deserves its own pass rather than being folded into this one — the profile page at least carries Tony’s own Pro-gate banner above it, which the home card did not.
  • Messages and Reminders became rail destinations, 14 Sep [T] [💡 rec · comp 14 Sep] — Tony, pinned on the Tools group: “Should we also add here Messages (coming soon) Reminder (coming soon)”. Messages was not a new ask. The page inventory’s row 1 carries his own answer from 31 Aug — “Show disabled. Maybe we can show ‘coming soon’ label” — and it sits on the do-not-re-ask list in [[stakeholder-questions]]; the first-session spec wrote it up as six items, Messages disabled with a coming soon label. We built a home card instead, so the content was carried and the placement was not, and this comment is him noticing a five-week-old decision we did not execute. That is the third of his comments today to turn out to be our compliance gap rather than his new idea, after the deal-checklist line that promised three fields where the form blocks on five, and the profile row whose gate he had already stated. Reminders is the genuinely new half — it arrived 31 Aug, after the rail was settled, and this is the first time he puts it in navigation. Twenty-six products on Mobbin argued with the one word disabled, and the build follows the evidence rather than the instruction. Thirteen keep an unavailable destination in the rail and clickable, letting the page carry the state: Docusign, Cursor, Plain, Peec AI and Cloudflare on paywalls; Duolingo, Copilot Labs, Teachable, Whop, Cofounder, Deputy, Juicebox and Airbnb on things not built or not yours. Nobody ships a permanently disabled nav row — Toggl’s greyed rail is a page-load state, and the only disabling in the whole sample is Copilot’s Coming Soon button on the destination, not the row that reached it. The reason the clickable pattern wins is structural: a disabled row has nowhere to put prose, so it can only ever say the noun, while a destination has a page. Our own first sketch proved the point by reaching for tooltips to carry the two sentences the home card already had. Two borrowed signals were refused. A Soon badge in the rail would sit in the exact slot where Docusign, Codecademy, GoDaddy, Toggl, Cloudflare and Plain put NEW and Beta, every one of which means shipped, go look. And a lock icon means you could have this if you paid in all five paywall cases — Messages is not behind a tier, it is unbuilt. Both would have said something false in a vocabulary the broker has learned elsewhere. The rows are marked all the same (Tanya, an hour later: “should we add ‘Soon’ badges on sidebar as well?”) — and the evidence alone says no: twelve of the thirteen leave the rail row bare and let the page explain, the lone exception being Docusign’s paywall padlock. Two things that sample was not weighing argue the other way. Tony wrote (coming soon) twice in one comment, and a demo audience reads the rail as the roadmap — which is a real job on a product being pitched, not a UX slip. And we have two dead ends side by side where the sample mostly has one, and where a paywall row wants to be clicked because clicking it is the sell; ours wants nothing. So the word goes in .ext, the quiet suffix slot Education’s ↗ already occupies, rather than in a badge. That keeps all three constraints: it reads as quiet, which is the half of his show disabled that survives contact with the evidence; it stays clickable, which is what the sample actually argues for; and it borrows nothing from the NEW/Beta vocabulary. The word, not a clock glyph — a clock reads as recent as readily as not yet, and Soon is his own. No new token was needed: .ext’s 55% composites to 4.73:1 on the rail’s #08142d, clearing AA for normal text, which matters the same week the rail’s trial countdown was lifted for contrast. One consequence accepted: the marker vanishes when the rail collapses, since the collapsed rail is icons alone — the same trade ↗ has always made, so it follows an existing decision rather than opening a new gap. What was built: two ordinary rail rows after Opportunities, in the main group rather than under Tools (Education is a tool; these are destinations), which restores the six-item rail the spec described. Each routes to a page carrying the feature name, a .badge --outline reading Coming soon on the h1 — Teachable’s NOT YET ENABLED pill, in this file’s own component — the sentence the home card used to hold, and an empty state saying Not available yet. One call to action, added an hour later (Tanya: “can we add some CTA on those page to [k]now that users [are] waiting for that functionality?”) — the first build had none, on the argument that every page in the sample offering a button is selling a tier or collecting an address it will really mail, and we would be doing neither. That reading missed a third job the same sample supports. Walmart’s Notify Me, Whop’s waitlist and Curater’s Request to be a curator sent ✓ are none of them sales — they measure want, and a feature nobody asks for is worth knowing about before it is built rather than after. So Notify me when it ships is the one filled control on the page, naming the address it would use, with the broker’s own email under it; the confirmed state is an .alert--success and a Take me off the list link, because a signal you cannot withdraw is not a signal. Per feature, not per page pair — wanting Messages says nothing about wanting Reminders. The toast carries the hole: there is no outbound mail anywhere in this prototype, so this is the third surface that would need one, after the lender invitation the add-a-contact form silently sends and the borrower document request. That is drawn the same way the document request was on 31 Aug — the state renders, and the toast says no message left the building — and it is the clearest argument yet for raising the mailer with Chris as one build rather than discovering it a screen at a time. [~] No date either. Cofounder’s Email is not yet available is the honest floor and this sits on it; Teachable’s check back soon and Whop’s we’ll notify you are claims about a schedule nobody here has, and the second is a mailer this prototype does not have either. [~] The home Coming soon card is gone, with its .qa row anatomy, under the same duplication rule that took the Start-here card on 4 Sep, the trial band’s button on 14 Sep and Browse lenders out of the checklist this morning. Announcing the same two features in the rail and in a card would have been the fourth instance in ten days. The badge was sitting 5.5px low (Tanya, minutes later, two crops of the two titles) — an inline chip aligns its own baseline to the line’s, and a 23.4px chip baseline-matched to a 26px cap lands well under the cap’s optical centre. This is the same defect .lpid was corrected for on the lender contact header, one size up, and it was fixed there with transform: translateY(-4.9px). That answer is wrong at this scale: .head h1 drops to 21px at 900px, and the raise a baseline-aligned chip needs scales with cap height, so a hard-coded value would be right at one size and wrong at the other. .head h1:has(.badge) is flex with align-items: center instead, which costs nothing in accuracy — Inter’s ascent and descent are near-symmetric about the cap centre at this leading, so the line-box centre is the cap centre, measured residual 0.1px — and is correct at every size by construction. The file had already reached the same answer once: .profhd h1 has been flex, centred, gapped since the profile was built, for the ⓘ that rides those titles. So this is adoption of an existing convention rather than a new rule, which is the third time in two days that the fix has been use what is already here — after the Checkbox and the Badge in the filter rail. One thing to correct elsewhere: [[first-session-screens-spec]] still specs Messages as disabled, which the build now contradicts on purpose. The spec should carry the Mobbin finding rather than be quietly out of step with the file. [~]
  • The lender clock left the row and became a column, 14 Sep (Tanya: “we can add column with date and hide it by default in settings”) [💡 rec] — every lender row carried active this month or last active N months ago, on four surfaces, all reading the same mo field. Three things were wrong with it at once. It broke this page’s own clock rule: past two weeks the question is this fresh? has one answer, so an absolute date takes over, and three months is well past two weeks. It never went quiet — active this month printed on the fresh records too, so all twenty-seven rows wore a clock and about twenty carried nothing. And it claimed more than the field holds: question 91 asked Tony what event makes a lender active and his answer was “I, as the Admin, must approve them” [T · 8 Sep], a one-time gate at registration that cannot say anything about this month. He had already deleted the sort built on the same field — “I don’t think we need this option”, 11 Sep — so the sub-line was the last surface still making the claim. Now: the sub-line is role and institution only, and the number lives in Profile updated, a column in the lenders table’s Settings popover, off by default. The header names the verb the record can actually support, which is the same gloss the profile’s stale-details warning already uses — one field, one meaning at last. The cell prints a month (Jun 2026) rather than a day, because mo is month-grained and a day would be invented precision. Why a hidden column rather than a quieter line: a row is for scanning and a profile is for acting, and the warning a broker needs before dialling a three-month-old number is already on the profile and in the drawer, which is where the dialling starts. The column is for the broker auditing freshness across the network, and that broker will go and switch it on. [~] If question 91 comes back saying the platform records a real activity event, this column keeps its place and gains a sibling; nothing here has to be undone.
  • Browse lenders left the setup checklist and became its own card, 14 Sep [T] — Tony, in a Figma comment pinned to that row on Home: “Browse Lenders should be an evergreen option vs. ‘get set up’ - it should be an independent box.” He is right, and the build was worse than a mislabelled row. A checklist is a completion widget, so every row needs a state where it is truthfully finished forever — and browsing lenders has none, so the predicate had to be faked. The other two rows read whether the thing exists (!gaps.length, DEALS.length > 0); this one read S.seenLenders, a flag the row’s own click handler set and nothing else touched, so done meant visited. And because the card retires itself once every row ticks, clicking the link once was what deleted it from Home. Measured across four states before touching it, counting doors to the lenders surface inside the Home region: first session 5, has deals and browsed once 4, everything done 3, and everything done with one opportunity open 2 — neither of them a door. The two survivors in that last state are the nav rail, which is not Home, and a KPI tile reading Lenders engaged · 7 across 4 deals, a metric about deals that happens to navigate there; the Browse lenders link in the nothing-needs-attention strip renders on !att.length && DEALS.length, so any attention row suppresses it. That state is not an edge case — it is the returning broker this page exists for. Now: the row is out of steps and S.seenLenders went with it, so the checklist is two rows whose predicates both read real data; a Lender network card takes the right column’s empty slot, where the retired entry-points card sat, always rendered with no done state and no dismissal. The three network figures moved into it from the first-session band [sandbox 3 Sep], which had the same evergreen failure one slot up: it rendered on !DEALS.length, so it vanished at the broker’s first deal. One change answers both. The 4 Sep duplication does not come back: checklist and entry points were collapsed into one slot that day because their rows were the same three destinations, and with this one gone they are no longer the same rows. [~] The card’s figure column is a fixed 72px rather than sized to content — 6, 7 and 7 glyphs started each label at a different x, and three rows that do not share a left edge read as three unrelated lines. [~] Q45 is still open and still governs the copy here — Browse lenders is the tracker’s own do-it-yourself wording. His comment does not answer that question but it constrains it, since an evergreen self-serve door on the dashboard is a do-it-yourself posture and sits badly beside “we handle lender matching, packaging, and follow-up”. The label stays as it is until he rules; only the container changed.
  • The ticker became a list, 14 Sep [T] [💡 rec · comp 14 Sep] — Tony, Figma comment on the network card, 9 Sep: “Should we add a scrolling ticker that lists the names of the institutions that are registered in the Lender Funnel / Lender Network just below this first row?” His own ask, twice — 13 Aug on the audit review call, already [agreed] in design-scope: “I do like the new registered lenders. We can put that somewhere on a ticker… just to advertise to brokers new lenders that join the platform. It’s a nice thing to have, but it’s not relative to how the system operates.” Never built. The two asks are not the same component: August is new registrations, a feed that stays short by construction; September is the institutions that are registered, a marquee of however many there are. Built as August’s. Thirty-three surfaces read on Mobbin and the split is clean.
